jorgensen_hilbert_2010.text: title = {A {H}ilbert Space Approach to Effective Resistance Metric}, volume = {4}, issn = {1661-8262}, url = {https://doi.org/10.1007/s11785-009-0041-1}, doi = {10.1007/s11785-009-0041-1}, abstract = {A resistance network is a connected graph (G, c). We show that the metric space (G, {RF}) embeds isometrically into \$\$\{\{{\textbackslash}mathcal H\}\_\{{\textbackslash}mathcal E\}\}\$\$, and the metric space (G, {RW}) embeds isometrically into the closure of the space of finitely supported functi

jayasumana_kernel_2013.text: title = {Kernel Methods on the Riemannian Manifold of Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices}, doi = {10.1109/CVPR.2013.17}, abstract = {Symmetric Positive Definite ({SPD}) matrices have become popular to encode image information. Accounting for the geometry of the Riemannian manifold of {SPD} matrices has proven key to the success of many algorithms. However, most existing methods only approximate the true shape of the manifold locally by its tangent plane. In this paper, inspired by kernel methods, we propose to map {SPD} matrices to a high dimensional Hilbert space where Euclidean geometry applies. To encode the geometry of the manifold in the mapping, we introduce a family of provably positive definite kernels on the Riemannian manifold of {SPD} matrices. These kernels are derived from the Gaussian kernel, but exploit different metrics on the manifold. This lets us extend kernel-based algorithms developed for Euclidean spaces, such as {SVM} and kernel {PCA}, to the Riemannian manifold of {SPD} matrices. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on the problems of pedestrian detection, object categorization, texture analysis, 2D motion segmentation and Diffusion Tensor Imaging ({DTI}) segmentation.}, eventtitle = {2013 {IEEE} Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition}, pages = {73--80}, booktitle = {2013 {IEEE} Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition}, author = {Jayasumana, Sadeep and Hartley, Richard and Salzmann, Mathieu and Li, Hongdong and Har

deza_geometry_1997.text: title = {Geometry of Cuts and Metrics}, abstract = {Cuts and metrics are well-known objects that arise - independently, but with many deep and fascinating connections - in diverse fields: in graph theory, combinatorial optimization, geometry of numbers, combinatorial matrix theory, statistical physics, {VLSI} design etc. This book offers a comprehensive summary together with a global view, establishing both old and new links. Its treatment ranges from classical theorems of Menger and Schoenberg to recent developments such as approximation results for multicommodity flow and max-cut problems, metric aspects of Delaunay polytopes, isometric graph embeddings, and matrix completion problems. The discussion leads to many interesting subjects that cannot be found elsewhere, providing a unique and invaluable source for researchers and graduate students.}, author = {Deza, Michel and Laurent, Monique}, date = {1997-01-01}, note = {Journal Abbreviation: Journal of Combinatorial Theory - {JCT} Publication Title: Journal of Combinatorial Theory - {JCT}}, file = {Full Text PDF:/home/tobia/snap/zotero-snap/common/Zotero/storage/FN3F2RDV/Deza and Laurent - 1997 - Geometry of Cuts and Metrics.pdf:application/pdf}, }

porcu2022nonseparable.text: author = {Porcu, Emilio and White, Philip A and Genton, Marc G}, title = "{Stationary nonseparable space-time covariance functions on networks}", journal = {Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology}, pages = {qkad082}, year = {2023}, month = {09}, abstract = "{The advent of data science has provided an increasing number of challenges with high data complexity. This paper addresses the challenge of space-time data where the spatial domain is not a planar surface, a sphere, or a linear network, but a generalised network (termed a graph with Euclidean edges). Additionally, data are repeatedly measured over different temporal instants. We provide new classes of stationary nonseparable space-time covariance functions where space can be a generalised network, a Euclidean tree, or a linear network, and where time can be linear or circular (seasonal). Because the construction principles are technical, we focus on illustrations that guide the reader through the construction of statistically interpretable examples. A simulation study demonstrates that the correct model can be recovered when compared to misspecified models. In addition, our simulation studies show that we effectively recover simulation parameters. In our data analysis, we consider a traffic accident dataset that shows improved model performance based on covariance specifications and network-based metrics.}", issn = {1369-7412}, doi = {10.1093/jrsssb/qkad082}, url = {https://doi.org/10.1

anderes_isotropic_2019.text: title = {Isotropic covariance functions on graphs and their edges}, url = {http://arxiv.org/abs/1710.01295}, doi = {10.48550/arXiv.1710.01295}, abstract = {We develop parametric classes of covariance functions on linear networks and their extension to graphs with Euclidean edges, i.e., graphs with edges viewed as line segments or more general sets with a coordinate system allowing us to consider points on the graph which are vertices or points on an edge. Our covariance functions are defined on the vertices and edge points of these graphs and are isotropic in the sense that they depend only on the geodesic distance or on a new metric called the resistance metric (which extends the classical resistance metric developed in electrical network theory on the vertices of a graph to the continuum of edge points). We discuss the advantages of using the resistance metric in comparison with the geodesic metric as well as the restrictions these metrics impose on the investigated covariance functions. In particular, many of the commonly used isotropic covariance functions in the spatial statistics literature (the power exponential, Mat\{{\textbackslash}'e\}rn, generalized Cauchy, and Dagum classes) are shown to be valid with respect to the resistance metric for any graph with Euclidean edges, whilst they are only valid with respect to the geodesic metric in more special cases.}, number = {{arXiv}:1710.01295}, publisher = {{arXiv}}, author = {Anderes, Ethan and Møller, Jesper and Rasmusse

takatsu_wasserstein_2011.text: title = {Wasserstein geometry of Gaussian measures}, volume = {48}, issn = {0030-6126}, url = {https://projecteuclid.org/journals/osaka-journal-of-mathematics/volume-48/issue-4/Wasserstein-geometry-of-Gaussian-measures/ojm/1326291215.full}, abstract = {This paper concerns the Riemannian/Alexandrov geometry of Gaussian measures, from the view point of the \$L{\textasciicircum}\{2\}\$-Wasserstein geometry. The space of Gaussian measures is of finite dimension, which allows to write down the explicit Riemannian metric which in turn induces the \$L{\textasciicircum}\{2\}\$-Wasserstein distance. Moreover, its completion as a metric space provides a complete picture of the singular behavior of the \$L{\textasciicircum}\{2\}\$-Wasserstein geometry. In particular, the singular set is stratified according to the dimension of the support of the Gaussian measures, providing an explicit nontrivial example of Alexandrov space with extremal sets.}, pages = {1005--1026}, number = {4}, journaltitle = {Osaka Journal of Mathematics}, author = {Takatsu, Asuka}, urldate = {2023-03-30}, date = {2011-12}, note = {Publisher: Osaka University and Osaka Metropolitan University, Departments of Mathematics}, file = {Full Text PDF:/home/tobia/snap/zotero-snap/common/Zotero/storage/JGPKE7ZV/Takatsu - 2011 - Wasserstein geometry of Gaussian measures.pdf:application/pdf}, }

bachoc_gaussian_2020.text: title = {Gaussian processes with multidimensional distribution inputs via optimal transport and Hilbertian embedding}, volume = {14}, issn = {1935-7524, 1935-7524}, url = {https://projecteuclid.org/journals/electronic-journal-of-statistics/volume-14/issue-2/Gaussian-processes-with-multidimensional-distribution-inputs-via-optimal-transport-and/10.1214/20-EJS1725.full}, doi = {10.1214/20-EJS1725}, abstract = {In this work, we propose a way to construct Gaussian processes indexed by multidimensional distributions. More precisely, we tackle the problem of defining positive definite kernels between multivariate distributions via notions of optimal transport and appealing to Hilbert space embeddings. Besides presenting a characterization of radial positive definite and strictly positive definite kernels on general Hilbert spaces, we investigate the statistical properties of our theoretical and empirical kernels, focusing in particular on consistency as well as the special case of Gaussian distributions. salmona_gromov-wasserstein_2021.text: title = {Gromov-Wasserstein Distances between Gaussian Distributions}, url = {http://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07970}, doi = {10.48550/arXiv.2104.07970}, abstract = {The Gromov-Wasserstein distances were proposed a few years ago to compare distributions which do not lie in the same space. In particular, they offer an interesting alternative to the Wasserstein distances for comparing probability measures living on Euclidean spaces of different dimensions. In this paper, we focus on the Gromov-Wasserstein distance with a ground cost defined as the squared Euclidean distance and we study the form of the optimal plan between Gaussian distributions. We show that when the optimal plan is restricted to Gaussian distributions, the problem has a very simple linear solution, which is also solution of the linear Gromov-Monge problem. We also study the problem without restriction on the optimal plan, and provide lower and upper bounds for the value of the Gromov-Wasserstein distance between Gaussian distributions.}, number = {{arXiv}:2104.07970}, publisher = {{arXiv}}, author = {Salmona, Antoine and Delon, Julie and Desolneux, Agnès}, urldate = {2023-03-31}, date = {2021-04-16}, eprinttype = {arxiv}, eprint = {2104.07970 [math]}, file = {arXiv Fulltext PDF:/home/tobia/snap/zotero-snap/common/Zotero/storage/ELM98JGM/Salmona et al. - 2021 - Gromov-Wasserstein Distances between Gaussian Dist.pdf:application/pdf;arXiv.org Snapshot:/home/tobia/snap/zotero-snap/common/Zotero/storage/4HINSN6D/2104.htm

janati_entropic_2020.text: title = {Entropic Optimal Transport between Unbalanced Gaussian Measures has a Closed Form}, url = {http://arxiv.org/abs/2006.02572}, doi = {10.48550/arXiv.2006.02572}, abstract = {Although optimal transport ({OT}) problems admit closed form solutions in a very few notable cases, e.g. in 1D or between Gaussians, these closed forms have proved extremely fecund for practitioners to define tools inspired from the {OT} geometry. On the other hand, the numerical resolution of {OT} problems using entropic regularization has given rise to many applications, but because there are no known closed-form solutions for entropic regularized {OT} problems, these approaches are mostly algorithmic, not informed by elegant closed forms. In this paper, we propose to fill the void at the intersection between these two schools of thought in {OT} by proving that the entropy-regularized optimal transport problem between two Gaussian measures admits a closed form. Contrary to the unregularized case, for which the explicit form is given by the Wasserstein-Bures distance, the closed form we obtain is differentiable everywhere, even for Gaussians with degenerate covariance matrices. We obtain this closed form solution by solving the fixed-point equation behind Sinkhorn's algorithm, the default method for computing entropic regularized {OT}. Remarkably, this approach extends to the generalized unbalanced case -- where Gaussian measures are scaled by positive constants. This extension leads to a closed f

mallasto_learning_2017.text: title = {Learning from uncertain curves: The 2-Wasserstein metric for Gaussian processes}, url = {https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Learning-from-uncertain-curves%3A-The-2-Wasserstein-Mallasto-Feragen/e3b8950e340a73750d7fd2c5b586b744c1314dbd}, shorttitle = {Learning from uncertain curves}, abstract = {We introduce a novel framework for statistical analysis of populations of non-degenerate Gaussian processes ({GPs}), which are natural representations of uncertain curves. This allows inherent variation or uncertainty in function-valued data to be properly incorporated in the population analysis. Using the 2-Wasserstein metric we geometrize the space of {GPs} with L2 mean and covariance functions over compact index spaces. We prove uniqueness of the barycenter of a population of {GPs}, as well as convergence of the metric and the barycenter of their finite-dimensional counterparts. This justifies practical computations. Finally, we demonstrate our framework through experimental validation on {GP} datasets representing brain connectivity and climate development. A Matlab library for relevant computations will be published at https://sites.google.com/view/antonmallasto/software.}, eventtitle = {{NIPS}}, author = {Mallasto, Anton and Feragen, A.}, urldate = {2023-03-31}, date = {2017}, }

senoussi_nonstationary_2021.text: title = {Nonstationary Space‐time Covariance Functions induced by Dynamical Systems}, volume = {49}, doi = {10.1111/sjos.12513}, abstract = {This paper provides a novel approach to nonstationarity by considering a bridge between differential equations and spatial fields. We consider the dynamical transformation of a given spatial process undergoing the action of a temporal flow of space diffeomorphisms. Such dynamical deformations are shown to be connected to certain classes of ordinary and partial differential equations. The natural question arises of how such dynamical diffeomorphisms convert the original spatial covariance function, specifically if the original covariance is spatially stationary or isotropic. We first challenge this question from a general perspective, and then turn into the special cases of both d‐dimensional Euclidean spaces, and hyperspheres. Several examples of dynamical diffeomorphisms defined in these spaces are given and some emphasis has been put on the stationary reducibility problem. porcu_space-time_2018.text: title = {Space-Time Geostatistical Models with both Linear and Seasonal Structures in the Temporal Components}, abstract = {We provide a novel approach to model space-time random fields where the temporal argument is decomposed into two parts. The former captures the linear argument, which is related, for instance, to the annual evolution of the field. The latter is instead a circular variable describing, for instance, monthly observations. The basic intuition behind this construction is to consider a random field defined over space (a compact set of the d-dimensional Euclidean space) across time, which is considered as the product space R × S1, with S1 being the unit circle. Under such framework, we derive new parametric families of covariance functions. In particular, we focus on two classes of parametric families. The former being parenthetical to the Gneiting class of covariance functions. The latter is instead obtained by proposing a new Lagrangian framework for the space-time domain considered in the manuscript. Our findings are illustrated through a real dataset of surface air temperatures. We show that the incorporation of both temporal variables can produce significant improvements in the predictive performances of the model. We also discuss the extension of this approach for fields defined spatially on a sphere, which allows to model space-time phenomena over large portions of planet Earth.}, type = {Non published article}, howpublished = {Non published article}, au

tang_space-time_2020.text: title = {Space-time covariance models on networks with an application on streams}, abstract = {The second-order, small-scale dependence structure of a stochastic process defined in the space-time domain is key to prediction (or kriging). While great efforts have been dedicated to developing models for cases in which the spatial domain is either a finite-dimensional Euclidean space or a unit sphere, counterpart developments on a generalized linear network are practically non-existent. To fill this gap, we develop a broad range of parametric, non-separable space-time covariance models on generalized linear networks and then an important subgroup -- Euclidean trees by the space embedding technique -- in concert with the generalized Gneiting class of models and 1-symmetric characteristic functions in the literature, and the scale mixture approach. We give examples from each class of models and investigate the geometric features of these covariance functions near the origin and at infinity. We also show the linkage between different classes of space-time covariance models on Euclidean trees. We illustrate the use of models constructed by different methodologies on a daily stream temperature data set and compare model predictive performance by cross validation.}, journal = {{arXiv}: Methodology}, author = {Tang, Jun and Zimmerman, D.}, urldate = {2023-06-09}, date = {2020-09-30}, year = {2020}, }

porcu_nested_2022.text: title = {Nested covariance functions on graphs with Euclidean edges cross time}, volume = {16}, issn = {1935-7524, 1935-7524}, url = {https://projecteuclid.org/journals/electronic-journal-of-statistics/volume-16/issue-2/Nested-covariance-functions-on-graphs-with-Euclidean-edges-cross-time/10.1214/22-EJS2039.full}, doi = {10.1214/22-EJS2039}, abstract = {Covariance functions over generalized networks have been explored to a very limited extent. We consider nested spatial or space-time covariance models, where space is a generalized network, and where time can be linear (the real line) or circular. We show sufficient conditions allowing preservation of positive semidefiniteness when at least one of the weights involved in the linear combination is negative. robins_random_2001.text: title = {Random graph models for temporal processes in social networks*}, volume = {25}, issn = {0022-250X, 1545-5874}, url = {http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0022250X.2001.9990243}, doi = {10.1080/0022250X.2001.9990243}, abstract = {We generalize the graphical modeling approach of p* social influence models to develop discrete time models for the temporal evolution of social networks. Plausible general processes pertaining to network evolution are broadly discussed as a basis for across‐time dependence assumptions. Systematic temporal processes are construed as effects that are homogeneous across the network, and that reflect dynamics inherent in a particular social relation. Any one actor cannot control these dynamics, especially given that non‐dyadic configurations may be implicated, for instance, tendencies for various triadic configurations to be constructed or to collapse of over time. Non‐systematic processes, on the other hand, may pertain to the changing nature of a particular dyadic tie, or to change involving a particular sociotemporal neighborhood of the network. Non‐systematic processes are inhomogeneous across time and across the network, and are modeled as random. In constructing p* dependence graphs, systematic temporal processes may be represented, in part, by the perfect dependence assumption, whereby network across‐time dependencies “mirror” within‐time dependencies. We develop temporal perfect dependence models appropriate for Markov random grap

hanneke_discrete_2010-1.text: title = {Discrete temporal models of social networks}, volume = {4}, issn = {1935-7524, 1935-7524}, url = {https://projecteuclid.org/journals/electronic-journal-of-statistics/volume-4/issue-none/Discrete-temporal-models-of-social-networks/10.1214/09-EJS548.full}, doi = {10.1214/09-EJS548}, abstract = {We propose a family of statistical models for social network evolution over time, which represents an extension of Exponential Random Graph Models ({ERGMs}). Many of the methods for {ERGMs} are readily adapted for these models, including maximum likelihood estimation algorithms. We discuss models of this type and their properties, and give examples, as well as a demonstration of their use for hypothesis testing and classification. We believe our temporal {ERG} models represent a useful new framework for modeling time-evolving social networks, and rewiring networks from other domains such as gene regulation circuitry, and communication networks.}, pages = {585--605}, issue = {none}, journaltitle = {Electronic Journal of Statistics}, author = {Hanneke, Steve and Fu, Wenjie and Xing, Eric P.}, urldate = {2023-05-25}, date = {2010-01}, note = {Publisher: Institute of Mathematical Statistics and Bernoulli Society}, file = {Full Text PDF:/home/tobia/snap/zotero-snap/common/Zotero/storage/6TXCRIB6/Hanneke et al. - 2010 - Discrete temporal models of social networks.pdf:application/pdf}, }

zhong_heterogeneous_2021.text: title = {Heterogeneous Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolution Network for Traffic Forecasting with Missing Values}, doi = {10.1109/ICDCS51616.2021.00073}, abstract = {Accurate traffic prediction is indispensable for intelligent traffic management. The availability of large-scale road sensing data collected by connected wireless sensors and mobile devices have provided unrealized potential for traffic prediction. However, sensory data is often incomplete due to various factors in the process of data acquisition and transmission. The missingness of traffic data brings a key challenge to the traffic prediction task since the state-of-the-art {ML}-based traffic prediction models (e.g., Graph Convolutional Networks ({GCN})) often rely on spatial and temporal completion of the data. Moreover, existing {GCN}-based methods usually build a static graph based on geographical distances and are limited in their ability to capture the time-evolving relationships amongst road segments. In this paper, we develop a heterogeneous spatio-temporal prediction framework for traffic prediction using incomplete historical data. In the framework, we build multiple graphs to explicitly model the dynamic correlations among road segments from both geographical and historical aspects, and employ recurrent neural networks to capture temporal correlations for each road segment. We impute missing values in a recurrent process, which is seamlessly embedded in the prediction framework so they can be jointly train

lee_model-based_2022.text: title = {Model-based clustering of semiparametric temporal exponential-family random graph models}, volume = {11}, issn = {2049-1573}, url = {https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/sta4.459}, doi = {10.1002/sta4.459}, abstract = {Model-based clustering of time-evolving networks has emerged as one of the important research topics in statistical network analysis. It is a fundamental research question to model time-varying network parameters. However, due to difficulties in modelling functional network parameters, there is little progress in the current literature to model time-varying network parameters effectively. In this work, we model network parameters as univariate nonparametric functions instead of constants. We effectively estimate those functional network parameters in temporal exponential-family random graph models using a kernel regression technique and a local likelihood approach. Furthermore, we propose a semiparametric finite mixture of temporal exponential-family random graph models by adopting finite mixture models, which simultaneously allows both modelling and detecting groups in time-evolving networks. Also, we use a conditional likelihood to construct an effective model selection criterion and network cross-validation to choose an optimal bandwidth. The power of our method is demonstrated in simulation studies and real-world applications to dynamic international trade networks and dynamic arm trade networks.}, pages = {e459}, number = {1}, journalti

ellens_effective_2011.text: title = {Effective graph resistance}, volume = {435}, issn = {0024-3795}, url = {https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379511001443}, series = {Special Issue in Honor of Dragos Cvetkovic}, abstract = {This paper studies an interesting graph measure that we call the effective graph resistance. The notion of effective graph resistance is derived from the field of electric circuit analysis where it is defined as the accumulated effective resistance between all pairs of vertices. The objective of the paper is twofold. First, we survey known formulae of the effective graph resistance and derive other representations as well. The derivation of new expressions is based on the analysis of the associated random walk on the graph and applies tools from Markov chain theory. This approach results in a new method to approximate the effective graph resistance. A second objective of this paper concerns the optimisation of the effective graph resistance for graphs with given number of vertices and diameter, and for optimal edge addition. A set of analytical results is described, as well as results obtained by exhaustive search. One of the foremost applications of the effective graph resistance we have in mind, is the analysis of robustness-related problems. However, with our discussion of this informative graph measure we hope to open up a wealth of possibilities of applying the effective graph resistance to all kinds of networks problems.}, pages = {2491--2506}, number = {1

monnig_resistance_2018.text: title = {The resistance perturbation distance: A metric for the analysis of dynamic networks}, volume = {236}, issn = {0166-218X}, url = {https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X17304626}, doi = {10.1016/j.dam.2017.10.007}, shorttitle = {The resistance perturbation distance}, abstract = {To quantify the fundamental evolution of time-varying networks, and detect abnormal behavior, one needs a notion of temporal difference that captures significant organizational changes between two successive instants. In this work, we propose a family of distances that can be tuned to quantify structural changes occurring on a graph at different scales: from the local scale formed by the neighbors of each vertex, to the largest scale that quantifies the connections between clusters, or communities. Our approach results in the definition of a true distance, and not merely a notion of similarity. We propose fast (linear in the number of edges) randomized algorithms that can quickly compute an approximation to the graph metric. The third contribution involves a fast algorithm to increase the robustness of a network by optimally decreasing the Kirchhoff index. Bevilacqua2016.text: author="Bevilacqua, Moreno and Alegria, Alfredo and Velandia, Daira and Porcu, Emilio", title="Composite Likelihood Inference for Multivariate {G}aussian Random Fields", journal="Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics", year="2016", volume="21", number="3", pages="448--469", abstract="In the recent years, there has been a growing interest in proposing covariance models for multivariate Gaussian random fields. Some of these covariance models are very flexible and can capture both the marginal and the cross-spatial dependence of the components of the associated multivariate Gaussian random field. However, effective estimation methods for these models are somehow unexplored. Maximum likelihood is certainly a useful tool, but it is impractical in all the circumstances where the number of observations is very large. In this work, we consider two possible approaches based on composite likelihood for multivariate covariance model estimation. We illustrate, through simulation experiments, that our methods offer a good balance between statistical efficiency and computational complexity. Asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators are assessed under increasing domain asymptotics. Finally, we apply the method for the analysis of a bivariate dataset on chlorophyll concentration and sea surface temperature in the Chilean coast.", issn="1537-2693", doi="10.1007/s13253-016-0256-3", url="http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s13253-016-0256-3" }

Baxevani1.text: author="Baxevani, Anastassia and Podg{\'o}rski, Krzysztof and Rychlik, Igor", title="Dynamically evolving {G}aussian spatial fields", journal="Extremes", year="2011", month="Jun", day="01", volume="14", number="2", pages="223--251", abstract="We discuss general non-stationary spatio-temporal surfaces that involve dynamics governed by velocity fields. The approach formalizes and expands previously used models in analysis of satellite data of significant wave heights. We start with homogeneous spatial fields. By applying an extension of the standard moving average construction we obtain models which are stationary in time. The resulting surface changes with time but is dynamically inactive since its velocities, when sampled across the field, have distributions centered at zero. We introduce a dynamical evolution to such a field by composing it with a dynamical flow governed by a given velocity field. This leads to non-stationary models. The models are extensions of the earlier discretized autoregressive models which account for a local velocity of traveling surface. We demonstrate that for such a surface its dynamics is a combination of dynamics introduced by the flow and the dynamics resulting from the covariance structure of the underlying stochastic field. We extend this approach to fields that are only locally stationary and have their parameters varying over a larger spatio-temporal horizon.", issn="1572-915X", doi="10.1007/s10687-010-0120-8", url="https://doi.org/10.1007/

nodes.name: p-variate Gaussian random field on a metric graph
nodes.statement: The purpose of the work is to construct a $p$-variate Gaussian {random field}, denoted $\rVec{Z}:= \{ \rVec{Z}(u)=(Z_1(u),\ldots,Z_p(u))^{\top}, \; u \in {\cal G} \}$ throughout and defined over a metric graph, $\mathcal G$, with a given matrix-valued covariance function that is isotropic, that is it depends on the {\em distance} between the points of the graph.
nodes.statement_short: Goal object: a p-variate Gaussian random field Z on a metric graph G with isotropic matrix-valued covariance.

nodes.name: Covariance as function of matrix-valued distance
nodes.statement: \latMatr K(u,v):= \psi \left ( \latMatr D(u,v) \right ), \qquad u,v \in \mathcal G,
nodes.label: eq:covariance_general

nodes.name: Matrix-valued composition covariance
nodes.statement: \latMatr{K}(u,v):= \grMatr{\Psi} \left ( \latMatr{D}(u,v) \right ) = \left [ \Psi_{ij}(D_{ij}(u,v)) \right ]_{i,j=1}^p, \qquad u,v \in \mathcal G,
nodes.label: eq:covariance_general_2

nodes.name: Number of variables p
nodes.statement: Throughout, $p$ is an integer greater than $1$ (the case $p=1$ has been treated by \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}).

nodes.name: Transpose and Moore-Penrose inverse notation
nodes.statement: $\latMatr{A}^\top$, $\dVec{\delta}^\top$ and $\rVec{Z}^\top$ are the transposes of $\latMatr{A}$, $\dVec{\delta}$ and $\rVec{Z}$, while $\latMatr{A}^-$ stands for the Moore-Penrose inverse of $\latMatr{A}$.

nodes.name: All-ones vector, all-ones matrix and identity notation
nodes.statement: The all-ones vector of size $n$, all-ones matrix of size $n \times n$, {and identity matrix of size $n\times n$} are denoted as ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, ${\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ and $\latMatr{I}_n$, respectively.

nodes.name: Matrix J_n
nodes.statement: Finally, we define $\latMatr{J}_n := \mathrm{diag}{[ 0, 0, \dots, 0, 1]^\top}$ ($n \times n$ diagonal matrix with only one non-zero entry).

nodes.name: Element-wise convention for functions of matrices
nodes.statement: Continuity, differentiation, integration and scalar- or matrix-valued functions (except power functions) involving matrices are understood as being performed element-wise.

nodes.name: Matrix power and principal square root convention
nodes.statement: Concerning the power functions, $\latMatr{A}^2$ is $\latMatr{A}$ multiplied by itself, $\sqrt{\latMatr{A}}=\latMatr{A}^{1/2}$ is the principal square root of $\latMatr{A}$, and $\latMatr{A}^{-1}$ is the inverse of $\latMatr{A}$ in the matrix sense.

nodes.name: Zero-mean isotropic random field
nodes.statement: We assume a {random field} with zero-mean vector and with a matrix-valued covariance matrix $\latMatr K: \mathcal G \times \mathcal G \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ that is isotropic in the sense there exists a pair $(\grMatr \Psi, \latMatr D)$, with $\grMatr \Psi: [0,+\infty)^{p \times p} \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ and $\latMatr D : \mathcal G \times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p \times p}$, both continuous, such that Equation (\ref{eq:covariance_general_2}) is satisfied.
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement_short: Z has zero mean and a covariance K(u,v)=Psi(D(u,v)) for continuous Psi and matrix-valued D.

nodes.name: Graph with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement: The type of topology considered by \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020} (to which the reader is referred for additional details and motivation) is called graph {\em with Euclidean edges}, denoted with a triple ${\cal G}=\left( V,E,\{\varphi_e\}_{e\in E} \right)$ throughout, where the elements are blended in the following way: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] {{$(V, E)$}} has a graph structure, \textit{i.e. } $V$ is the set of vertices and {$E\subset V\times V$} accounts for the edges. We assume that this graph is simple and connected, \textit{i.e. } $V$ is finite, the graph has not repeated edges or edges that join a vertex to itself and every pair of vertices is connected by a path. \item[(b)] Each edge $e\in E$ is provided with a \emph{length} $\ell(e)>0$ and a \emph{weight} $w(e):=1/\ell(e)$; furthermore, it is associated with a unique abstract set, also denoted $e$, such that $V$ and all the edge sets are mutually disjoint. \item[(c)] Let $v_1$ and $v_2$ be vertices connected by $e\in E$. Then, $\varphi_e$ is a continuous and bijective mapping defined on $e \cup \{v_1,v_2\}$, such that $\varphi_e$ maps $e$ onto an open interval $(0,\ell(e)) \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $\{v_1,v_2\}$ onto $\{0,\ell(e)\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement_short: A simple connected graph whose edges carry lengths and are bijectively mapped to real intervals (0, l(e)).
nodes.label: def:graphWithEE

nodes.name: Total order on vertices and edge orientation
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we shall assume the existence of a total order relation on the set of vertices $V$ and that every edge is represented through the ordered pair $(v_1,v_2)$, where $v_1<v_2$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges

nodes.name: Point representation u = (u_lower, u_upper, delta)
nodes.statement: {By abuse of notation, we write} {$u\in\mathcal G$ to denote a point on the graph: it can be either a vertex or a point on an edge. Each point $u\in \mathcal G$ will be identified with the triple $(\ul u, \ol u, \delta)$, where: $\ul u < \ol u$ are the endpoints of the edge $e$ containing $u$ and $\delta \in [0,1]$ is the relative distance of $u$ from $\ul u$; formally: $\delta=\delta(u):=w(e)\varphi_e(u)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement_short: A point u of G is identified by its edge endpoints and its relative position delta(u) in [0,1] along the edge.

nodes.name: Edge map e(u)
nodes.statement: Finally, we use the notation $e(u)$, where $e:\mathcal G \to E$, to denote the edge that contains $u$. If $u\in V$, then $e(u)$ is any of the edges that have an endpoint in $u$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges

nodes.name: Euclidean tree
nodes.statement: A graph with Euclidean edges is called an \emph{Euclidean tree} if it has a tree structure, \textit{i.e. } given any two points $u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal{G}$, there is exactly one path that connects $u_1$ to $u_2$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges

nodes.name: Leaf of a Euclidean tree
nodes.statement: {A vertex of a Euclidean tree is called a \emph{leaf} if it is connected to only one other vertex.}
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges
differentia: it is connected to only one other vertex

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite and conditionally negative semidefinite matrices
nodes.statement: An $n\times n$ real matrix $\latMatr A$ is said to be \emph{positive semidefinite} if and only if $\dVec{c}^\top \latMatr{A} \dVec{c} \geq 0$ for all $\dVec{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and \emph{conditionally negative semidefinite} if and only if $\dVec{c}^\top \latMatr{A} \dVec{c} \leq 0$ for all $\dVec{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top \dVec{c} = 0$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Classes of matrices used in the paper

nodes.name: Quasi-Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: An $n\times n$ matrix $\latMatr L$ is called \emph{quasi-Laplacian} if and only if it is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and has exactly one null eigenvalue, with corresponding eigenvector ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Classes of matrices used in the paper
differentia: has exactly one null eigenvalue, with corresponding eigenvector ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$

nodes.name: Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: A quasi-Laplacian matrix $\latMatr L$ is called \emph{Laplacian} if and only if it has non-positive off-diagonal entries.
nodes.section: 2.3 Classes of matrices used in the paper

nodes.name: Laplacian matrix of a graph with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we will consider the Laplacian matrix of a given graph with Euclidean edges, with entries defined as \citet[Equation (1)]{devriendt_effective_2022}: {\begin{equation} L_{ij} = \begin{dcases} \sum_{v\in V} w((v, v_i)) &\text{ if $i=j$}\\ -w((v_i,v_j)) &\text{ if $i \neq j$,} \end{dcases} \end{equation} with $w((v_i,v_j))$ the weight of the edge joining vertices $v_i$ and $v_j$ if these vertices are connected, $0$ otherwise.}
nodes.section: 2.3 Classes of matrices used in the paper
nodes.definiendum: Laplacian matrix of a graph with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement_short: The graph Laplacian: diagonal entries are sums of incident edge weights, off-diagonal entries minus the edge weight.

nodes.name: Laplacian of a graph
nodes.statement: L_{ij} = \begin{dcases} \sum_{v\in V} w((v, v_i)) &\text{ if $i=j$}\\ -w((v_i,v_j)) &\text{ if $i \neq j$,} \end{dcases}
nodes.section: 2.3 Classes of matrices used in the paper
nodes.label: eq:laplacianofagraph

nodes.name: Properties of quasi-Laplacian matrices
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr L$ be a quasi-Laplacian matrix partitioned as follows: \begin{equation} {\latMatr{L}}=\begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}}^\top & {\latMatr{C}} \end{bmatrix}, \end{equation} where ${\latMatr{A}}$ and ${\latMatr{C}}$ are square matrices. Then the following statements hold. \begin{enumerate} \item ${\latMatr{B}}\ne \grMatr 0$. \item ${\latMatr{A}}$ and ${\latMatr{C}}$ are strictly positive definite. \item Both ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}:={\latMatr{A}}-{\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}^\top$ and ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{A}}:={\latMatr{C}} - {\latMatr{B}}^\top {\latMatr{A}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}$ are quasi-Laplacian matrices, \textit{i.e. }, the set of quasi-Laplacian matrices is closed under the Schur complement operation. \item ${\latMatr{L}}^-$ is a quasi-Laplacian matrix. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.3 Classes of matrices used in the paper
assumptions: Let $\latMatr L$ be a quasi-Laplacian matrix partitioned as follows:
where ${\latMatr{A}}$ and ${\latMatr{C}}$ are square matrices.
conclusions: the set of quasi-Laplacian matrices is closed under the Schur complement operation.
nodes.statement_short: For a partitioned quasi-Laplacian matrix: off-diagonal block nonzero, diagonal blocks positive definite, Schur complements and Moore-Penrose inverse are quasi-Laplacian.
nodes.label: prop:quasiLaplacianProperties

nodes.name: Partition of a quasi-Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: {\latMatr{L}}=\begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}}^\top & {\latMatr{C}} \end{bmatrix},
nodes.section: 2.3 Classes of matrices used in the paper
nodes.label: eq:partitionQuasiLapl

nodes.name: Variogram
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set and $Z:X\to \mathbb{R}$ a square-integrable random {field}. The \emph{variogram} of $Z$ is defined via \begin{align} \gamma_{{Z}}: X\times X &\to \mathbb{R} \nonumber\\ (x_1,x_2)&\mapsto \gamma_{{Z}} (x_1,x_2):=\mathbb{V}ar\round{{Z}(x_1)-{Z}(x_2)}.\nonumber \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The variogram of Z is gamma(x1,x2)=Var(Z(x1)-Z(x2)).

nodes.name: Variogram is conditionally negative semidefinite
nodes.statement: Clearly, a variogram is always symmetric and non-negative valued. In addition, it is conditionally negative semidefinite, \textit{i.e. } it satisfies \citep{chiles2012geostatistics} \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j \gamma(x_i,x_j) \leq 0 \end{equation} whenever $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i = 0$, for any $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$.
assumptions: whenever $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i = 0$, for any $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$
conclusions: a variogram is always symmetric and non-negative valued

nodes.name: Conditional negative semidefiniteness of variograms
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j \gamma(x_i,x_j) \leq 0

nodes.name: Resistance metric
nodes.statement: \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020} define the resistance metric, denoting $d_R$ throughout, as the variogram of a {random field} $Z$ on the graph with Euclidean edges $\mathcal G$, that is constructed {\em ad hoc} in order to be as much as possibly parenthetical to a Brownian bridge on the graph.
nodes.statement_short: d_R is the variogram of an ad hoc Brownian-bridge-like random field on the graph with Euclidean edges.

nodes.name: Pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: The concept of variogram can be generalised to the case of a zero-mean square-integrable vector-valued random field $\rVec{Z}$ on a non-empty set $X$, through the following lines. The \emph{pseudo-variogram} of $\rVec{Z}$ is defined through the identity \begin{align} \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}:X\times X &\to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}\nonumber \\ (x_1,x_2) &\mapsto \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(x_1,x_2):=\Big [ \mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(x_1)-Z_j(x_2)} \Big ]_{i,j=1}^p. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The pseudo-variogram of a vector field Z is the matrix [Var(Z_i(x1)-Z_j(x2))]_{ij}.

nodes.name: Pseudo-variogram definition
nodes.statement: \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}:X\times X &\to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}\nonumber \\ (x_1,x_2) &\mapsto \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(x_1,x_2):=\Big [ \mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(x_1)-Z_j(x_2)} \Big ]_{i,j=1}^p.
nodes.label: eq:pseudoVariogramDef

nodes.name: Matrix form of the pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: Straightforward calculations allow to rewrite the above as \begin{equation} \grMatr \Gamma_{\boldsymbol{Z}}(x_1,x_2) = \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)} \,{\mathbf{1}_{p}}^\top + {\mathbf{1}_{p}}\, \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}^\top - 2\, \Cov{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)}{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}, \end{equation} where $\mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ is the $p\times p$ {collocated} variance-covariance matrix of $\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$, $\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ is the $p\times 1$ vector containing the main diagonal of $\mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ and $\Cov{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)}{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}:=\Exp{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)^\top}$.
assumptions: where $\mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ is the $p\times p$ {collocated} variance-covariance matrix of $\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$
conclusions: Straightforward calculations allow to rewrite the above as
nodes.statement_short: Pseudo-variogram = diag variances of each point spread over rows/columns minus twice the cross-covariance.

nodes.name: Pseudo-variogram in matrix form
nodes.statement: \grMatr \Gamma_{\boldsymbol{Z}}(x_1,x_2) = \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)} \,{\mathbf{1}_{p}}^\top + {\mathbf{1}_{p}}\, \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}^\top - 2\, \Cov{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)}{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)},
nodes.label: eq:pseudoVariogramMatricial

nodes.name: Properties of the pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: The pseudo-variogram satisfies the following properties \citep{dorr2023characterization}: \begin{itemize} \item {for any $x_1,x_2 \in X$,} \begin{equation} \grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_1,x_2)=\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_2,x_1)^\top; \end{equation} \item {for any $x \in X$, the diagonal entries of $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x,x)$ are zero;} \item $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}$ is ${\mathbf{1}_{p}}$-conditionally negative semidefinite, \textit{i.e. } for all {$n \in \mathbb{N}^+$, $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$ and } $\dVec c_1,\dots,\dVec c_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$ such that $ {{\mathbf{1}_{p}}}^\top \sum_{i=1}^n \dVec c_i = 0$, it holds \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec c_i^\top \grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_i,x_j) \dVec c_j \leq 0. \end{equation} \end{itemize}
conclusions: for any $x \in X$, the diagonal entries of $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x,x)$ are zero;
nodes.statement_short: A pseudo-variogram is transpose-symmetric, has zero diagonal at coincident points, and is 1_p-conditionally negative semidefinite.

nodes.name: Transpose symmetry of the pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: \grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_1,x_2)=\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_2,x_1)^\top;
nodes.label: sympseudo

nodes.name: 1_p-conditional negative semidefiniteness
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec c_i^\top \grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_i,x_j) \dVec c_j \leq 0.
nodes.label: eq:negativesemidef

nodes.name: Multivariate distance via pseudo-variogram (general set)
nodes.statement: In the following, we define the multivariate distance $\latMatr D:X\times X \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}$ via $\latMatr D(x_1,x_2):=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{\latMatr L}(x_1,x_2)$.

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite function
nodes.statement: A function $k:X\times X \to \mathbb{R}$ is positive semidefinite if, for all $n\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$, ${x}_1,\dots,{x}_n \in X$ and $c_1,\dots,c_n \in \mathbb{R}$, one has \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j k({x}_i, {x}_j) \geq 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite function condition
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j k({x}_i, {x}_j) \geq 0.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations
nodes.label: eq:positSemiDefFunction

nodes.name: Strictly positive definite function
nodes.statement: In addition, $k$ is a strictly positive definite function if it is positive semidefinite and \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j) = 0 \implies c_1=\dots=c_n = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Strict positive definiteness condition
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j) = 0 \implies c_1=\dots=c_n = 0.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite matrix-valued function
nodes.statement: A matrix-valued function $\latMatr K :X\times X \to \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is positive semidefinite if, for all $n\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$, ${\dVec{c}}_1,\dots,{\dVec{c}}_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$ and ${x}_1,\dots,{x}_n\in X$, it holds: \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n {\dVec{c}}_i^\top \latMatr{K}(x_i,x_j) {\dVec{c}}_j \geq 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Matrix-valued positive semidefiniteness condition
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n {\dVec{c}}_i^\top \latMatr{K}(x_i,x_j) {\dVec{c}}_j \geq 0.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations
nodes.label: eq:positiveSemidef

nodes.name: Strictly positive definite matrix-valued function
nodes.statement: In addition, $\latMatr{K}$ is strictly positive definite if it is positive semidefinite and the condition \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n {\dVec{c}}_i^\top \latMatr K ({x}_i,{x}_j) {\dVec{c}}_j = 0 \end{equation} implies that there exists a pair $ i\ne j$ such that ${x}_i={x}_j$ or ${\dVec{c}}_1=\dots={\dVec{c}}_n=0$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Matrix-valued strict definiteness condition
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n {\dVec{c}}_i^\top \latMatr K ({x}_i,{x}_j) {\dVec{c}}_j = 0
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Block-matrix characterisation of positive semidefinite matrix-valued functions
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr{K} : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$. Then, {the following} are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item $\latMatr{K}$ is positive semidefinite; \item for all $n\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$ and for all ${x}_1,\dots, {x}_n\in X$, the $np \times np$ block matrix $\latMatr C:=[C_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^{np}:=[\latMatr{K}({x}_i,{x}_j)]_{i,j=1}^{{n}}$ is positive semidefinite, \textit{i.e. }, $\dVec{c}^\top \latMatr C \dVec{c} \geq 0$ for any $\dVec{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{np}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations
assumptions: Let $\latMatr{K} : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$.
equivalent_conditions: for all $n\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$ and for all ${x}_1,\dots, {x}_n\in X$, the $np \times np$ block matrix $\latMatr C:=[C_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^{np}:=[\latMatr{K}({x}_i,{x}_j)]_{i,j=1}^{{n}}$ is positive semidefinite
nodes.statement_short: K is positive semidefinite iff every np x np block matrix [K(x_i,x_j)] is positive semidefinite.
nodes.label: prop:equivalentFormPositDef

nodes.name: Completely monotone function
nodes.statement: A function $\psi:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ is called \emph{completely monotone} if it is continuous on $[0,+\infty)$, infinitely differentiable on $(0,+\infty)$ and for each $i\in \mathbb{N}$ it holds \begin{equation*} (-1)^i\,\psi^{(i)}(x)\geq 0, \end{equation*} where $\psi^{(i)}$ denotes the $i^\text{th}$ derivative of $\psi$ and $\psi^{(0)}:=\psi$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Bernstein's characterisation of completely monotone functions
nodes.statement: A function $\psi:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ is completely monotone if and only if it is the Laplace transform of a (unique) finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $[0,+\infty)$, \textit{i.e. } \begin{equation} \psi(x)=\int_0^{+\infty} \exp(-tx) \, \mu({\rm d}t), \quad x\in [0,+\infty). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations
conclusions: is completely monotone if and only if it is the Laplace transform of a (unique) finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $[0,+\infty)$
equivalent_conditions: it is the Laplace transform of a (unique) finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $[0,+\infty)$

nodes.name: Laplace transform representation
nodes.statement: \psi(x)=\int_0^{+\infty} \exp(-tx) \, \mu({\rm d}t), \quad x\in [0,+\infty).
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations
nodes.label: eq:compMonotLaplaceTransform

nodes.name: Bernstein function
nodes.statement: A function $g:[0,+\infty) \to [0,+\infty)$ is called a \emph{Bernstein function} if $g$ in infinitely differentiable on $[0,+\infty)$ and $g^{(1)}$ is a completely monotone function.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Multivariate Schoenberg theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\psi: [0,+\infty)\to {(0,+\infty)}$ be a {non-constant} completely monotone function, $g:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ {be} a Bernstein function and let $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}: X\times X\to [0,+\infty)^{p\times p}$, for a non-empty set $X$. If, for all ${x_1,x_2}\in X$, $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}^\top(x_1,x_2)=\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_2,x_1)$ and $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}$ is ${\mathbf{1}_{p}}$-conditionally negative semidefinite, then, for all ${\xi}>0$, \begin{equation*} ({x_1,x_2})\mapsto \psi\Big ({\xi} \, g\round{\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}({x_1,x_2}}\Big ), \qquad {x_1,x_2}\in X, \end{equation*} where $\psi$ and $g$ are applied element-wise, is a positive semidefinite function on $X$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations
assumptions: Let $\psi: [0,+\infty)\to {(0,+\infty)}$ be a {non-constant} completely monotone function
$g:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ {be} a Bernstein function
for all ${x_1,x_2}\in X$, $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}^\top(x_1,x_2)=\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_2,x_1)$
$\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}$ is ${\mathbf{1}_{p}}$-conditionally negative semidefinite
conclusions: is a positive semidefinite function on $X$.
nodes.statement_short: psi(xi g(Gamma)) applied element-wise is positive semidefinite for completely monotone psi, Bernstein g and a 1_p-CNSD transpose-symmetric Gamma.
nodes.label: theo:MultivariateSchoenberg

nodes.name: Notation n, L, Sigma, Lambda, W and M_p
nodes.statement: The following notation will ease the exposition throughout: \begin{itemize} \item $n$ is the number of vertices of {the graph} ${\cal G}$ (cardinality of $V$), \item ${\latMatr{L}}$ is the Laplacian matrix of ${\cal G}$ as per Equation (\ref{eq:laplacianofagraph}), \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}:={\latMatr{L}}^-$ is the Moore-Penrose inverse of ${\latMatr{L}}$, \item ${\grMatr{\Lambda}}$ and ${\latMatr{W}}$ are the eigenvalues and eigenvectors matrices of ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}$, \textit{i.e. } ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = {\latMatr{W}} {\grMatr{\Lambda}} {\latMatr{W}}^\top$, \item for two matrices ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}$ {of the same size} and for a positive integer $p$, we define \begin{equation} \Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:={\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - {\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{A}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{A}} \end{bmatrix}. \end{equation} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: n vertices, Laplacian L, Sigma = L^- with eigendecomposition W Lambda W^T, and the block matrix M_p(A,B) with A on the diagonal and B off it.

nodes.name: Block matrix M_p(A,B)
nodes.statement: \Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:={\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - {\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{A}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{A}} \end{bmatrix}.
nodes.label: eq:notationM

nodes.name: Additive construction Z = Z_V + Z_E
nodes.statement: Specifically, we shall consider a vector-valued random field, $\rVec{Z}$, that is obtained through the identity \begin{equation} \rVec{Z}(u) := \rVec{Z}_{V}(u) + \rVec{Z}_{E}(u), \qquad u \in \mathcal G. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Random field as sum of vertex and edge fields
nodes.statement: \rVec{Z}(u) := \rVec{Z}_{V}(u) + \rVec{Z}_{E}(u), \qquad u \in \mathcal G.
nodes.label: eq:multivariate_random_field_Z

nodes.name: Desideratum D1: diagonal variograms as in Anderes et al.
nodes.statement: The construction (\ref{eq:multivariate_random_field_Z}) needs to provide a pseudo-variogram $\grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}$ for which the diagonal entries should obey to the variogram construction as in \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}.

nodes.name: Desideratum D2: block-precision matrix Theta
nodes.statement: The multivariate {random field} $\rVec{Z}_V$ on $V$ should enjoy a homogeneous conditional independence structure. More precisely, we set the block-precision matrix ${\grMatr{\Theta}}$ of $\rVec{Z}_V$ to have the following structure: \begin{equation} {\grMatr{\Theta}} = \Mv{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha {\latMatr{I}_n}}, \end{equation} where $\alpha$ is a positive real value and $\latMatr{Q}$ is a suitable $n\times n$ matrix that will be defined next. This means that, for $i\ne j$ and $v_1\ne v_2$, ${Z}_{V,i}(v_1)$ and $Z_{V,j}(v_2)$ are conditionally independent given everything else.
nodes.statement_short: Z_V on V has homogeneous conditional independence: its block precision is Theta = M_p(Q, -alpha I_n).

nodes.name: Block-precision matrix Theta
nodes.statement: {\grMatr{\Theta}} = \Mv{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha {\latMatr{I}_n}},
nodes.label: eq:defTheta

nodes.name: Matrices Q and X
nodes.statement: Define the $n\times n$ matrices: \begin{align} \latMatr{Q}&:=\frac{1}{2} \round{{\latMatr{L}}+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{\latMatr{L}^2-2\alpha (p-2){\latMatr{L}}+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2} {\latMatr{W}} \round{{\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{({\grMatr{\Lambda}}^{-})^2-2\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}} {\latMatr{W}}^\top,\\ {\latMatr{X}}&:=\frac{1}{\alpha(p-1)}\round{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr{Q} - {\latMatr{I}_n}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2\alpha (p-1)} {\latMatr{W}} \round{\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \sqrt{{\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n} - 2 \alpha (p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \alpha^2 p^2 {\grMatr{\Lambda}}^2} -{\latMatr{I}_n}-\latMatr{J}_n} {\latMatr{W}}^\top. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Q is a square-root expression in L, alpha and p; X = (Sigma Q - I)/(alpha(p-1)); both also given via the eigendecomposition of Sigma.

nodes.name: Definition of Q
nodes.statement: \latMatr{Q}&:=\frac{1}{2} \round{{\latMatr{L}}+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{\latMatr{L}^2-2\alpha (p-2){\latMatr{L}}+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2} {\latMatr{W}} \round{{\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{({\grMatr{\Lambda}}^{-})^2-2\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}} {\latMatr{W}}^\top,
nodes.label: eq:defQ

nodes.name: Definition of X
nodes.statement: {\latMatr{X}}&:=\frac{1}{\alpha(p-1)}\round{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr{Q} - {\latMatr{I}_n}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2\alpha (p-1)} {\latMatr{W}} \round{\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \sqrt{{\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n} - 2 \alpha (p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \alpha^2 p^2 {\grMatr{\Lambda}}^2} -{\latMatr{I}_n}-\latMatr{J}_n} {\latMatr{W}}^\top.
nodes.label: eq:defX

nodes.name: Spectral forms of Q and X
nodes.statement: Notice that in Equations (\ref{eq:defQEigen}) and (\ref{eq:defXEigen}) the principal square root coincides with the element-wise square root, being its arguments diagonal matrices. {These equations have been established from Equations (\ref{eq:defQ}) and (\ref{eq:defX}) by using the fact that $\latMatr{W}$ is an orthogonal matrix and that $\grMatr{\Lambda} \grMatr{\Lambda}^- = \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n$ insofar as the first $p-1$ diagonal entries of $\grMatr{\Lambda}$ are positive and the last diagonal entry is zero.}

nodes.name: Constants k_1, k_2 and matrices Sigma-tilde, X-tilde
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the two positive constants \begin{equation*} k_1 := \frac{p-1}{\alpha n p^2} \qquad k_2 := \frac{p^2-p+1}{\alpha n p^2(p-1)}, \end{equation*} and the $n \times n$ matrices \begin{equation*} \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} := {\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} \qquad \Tilde {\latMatr{X}} := {\latMatr{X}} + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the construction under the desiderata
nodes.statement: Although these definitions may appear {peculiar}, they are the only solution to the \emph{desiderata} $\mathbb D$ previously stated and are crucial to define the random field $\rVec{Z}_V$.
conclusions: they are the only solution to the \emph{desiderata} $\mathbb D$ previously stated

nodes.name: Covariance of Z_V on the vertices
nodes.statement: We start with the vertices, where $\rVec{Z}_V$ is assumed a zero-mean $p$-variate Gaussian random vector $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V:V\to \mathbb{R}^p$ having covariance matrix-valued function \begin{equation} \Cov{\rVec{Z}_V(v_1)}{\rVec{Z}_V(v_2)}:=\Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}[v_1, v_2]}{\Tilde {\latMatr{X}}[v_1, v_2]} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On vertices Z_V is a zero-mean Gaussian vector with covariance M_p(Sigma~[v1,v2], X~[v1,v2]).

nodes.name: Vertex covariance of Z_V
nodes.statement: \Cov{\rVec{Z}_V(v_1)}{\rVec{Z}_V(v_2)}:=\Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}[v_1, v_2]}{\Tilde {\latMatr{X}}[v_1, v_2]} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}.
nodes.label: eq:covZ_V_onV

nodes.name: Theta and its Moore-Penrose inverse are quasi-Laplacian
nodes.statement: The matrix $\grMatr \Theta$ defined in Equation (\ref{eq:defTheta}) and its Moore-Penrose inverse $\grMatr \Theta^-$ are quasi-Laplacian.
conclusions: The matrix $\grMatr \Theta$ defined in Equation (\ref{eq:defTheta}) and its Moore-Penrose inverse $\grMatr \Theta^-$ are quasi-Laplacian.
nodes.label: prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian

nodes.name: Vertex covariance is positive semidefinite
nodes.statement: The function defined in (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) is positive semidefinite.
conclusions: The function defined in (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) is positive semidefinite.
nodes.label: prop:covZ_V_isACov

nodes.name: Linear interpolation of Z_V on edges
nodes.statement: Once $\rVec{Z}_V$ is defined over the vertices, the corresponding values over the edges are attained through a sheer linear interpolation. Namely, for $u=(\ul u, \ol u,\delta(u))\in \mathcal G$, we set \begin{equation} \rVec{Z}_V(u):=(1-\delta(u)) \rVec{Z}_V(\ul u) + \delta(u) \rVec{Z}_V(\ol u). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Interpolation of Z_V
nodes.statement: \rVec{Z}_V(u):=(1-\delta(u)) \rVec{Z}_V(\ul u) + \delta(u) \rVec{Z}_V(\ol u).
nodes.label: eq:interpZv

nodes.name: Edge random field Z_E
nodes.statement: We define $\rVec{Z}_E$ as a $p$-variate zero-mean Gaussian random field independent of $\rVec{Z}_V$ whose covariance matrix-valued function is: \begin{equation} \Cov{\rVec{Z}_E(u_1)}{\rVec{Z}_E(u_2)}:=\mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}\Mv{p}{1}{\beta} \in {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}, \end{equation} for $e_i:=e(u_i)$, $\delta_i:={\delta}(u_i)$, $i\in\curly{1,2}$ and where $\beta\in\square{0,1}$ is a fixed parameter.
nodes.statement_short: Z_E is independent of Z_V, independent across edges, with Brownian-bridge covariance on each edge times M_p(1,beta).

nodes.name: Covariance of Z_E
nodes.statement: \Cov{\rVec{Z}_E(u_1)}{\rVec{Z}_E(u_2)}:=\mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}\Mv{p}{1}{\beta} \in {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p},
nodes.label: eq:covZ_E

nodes.name: Validity of the Z_E covariance
nodes.statement: Notice that $\rVec{Z}_E\big|_{e_1}$ is independent from $\rVec{Z}_E\big|_{e_2}$ whenever $e_1 \ne e_2$, in addition $\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}$ is the covariance function of a standard Brownian bridge on $[0,\ell(e_1)]$, whilst $\Mh{p}{1}{\beta}$ is positive semidefinite for $\beta\in[0,1]$. This ensures that (\ref{eq:covZ_E}) is positive semidefinite, as the {element-wise} product of positive semidefinite functions is itself positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: The Z_E covariance is psd: a Brownian-bridge covariance times the psd matrix M_p(1,beta), and Schur products preserve psd.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5 (from definitions)
nodes.statement: The following result comes directly from the above definitions.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation from the definitions of Z_V and Z_E.

nodes.name: Explicit covariances of Z_V and Z_E
nodes.statement: Let ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}$, ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}$ be the covariance mappings associated respectively with the {random fields} $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$. Then, it is true that \begin{equation} {\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)=\Mv{p}{\dVec{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}, \end{equation} for $u_i=(\ul u_i, \ol u_i, \delta_i)\in \mathcal G$ ($i\in\curly{1,2}$), and where $\dVec{\delta}_{{i,V}}$ is the $n$-dimensional vector whose entries are \begin{equation} {\delta}_{{i,{V}}}:=\begin{cases} 1-\delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ul u_i\\ \delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ol u_i\\ 0 \quad &\text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad v\in V. \end{equation} Further, it is true that \begin{equation*} {\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}(u_1,u_2)=\Mv{p}{\mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}. \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}$, ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}$ be the covariance mappings associated respectively with the {random fields} $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$.
nodes.statement_short: K_{Z_V} = M_p(delta1' Sigma~ delta2, delta1' X~ delta2) with interpolation weight vectors; K_{Z_E} = Brownian-bridge term times M_p(1,beta).
nodes.label: prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE

nodes.name: Covariance of Z_V at arbitrary points
nodes.statement: {\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)=\Mv{p}{\dVec{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p},

nodes.name: Interpolation weight vector delta_{i,V}
nodes.statement: {\delta}_{{i,{V}}}:=\begin{cases} 1-\delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ul u_i\\ \delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ol u_i\\ 0 \quad &\text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad v\in V.
nodes.label: eq:delta_i

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: As a direct implication of Proposition \ref{prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE} in concert with the fact that $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$ are independent, we obtain the following.
nodes.statement_short: Add the two covariances of Proposition 5, using independence of Z_V and Z_E.

nodes.name: Covariance of Z
nodes.statement: It is true that \begin{align} &{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)={\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)+{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}(u_1,u_2)\nonumber\\ &=\Mv{p}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}} + \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}} + \beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: K_Z is the sum of the Z_V and Z_E covariances, again of the block form M_p.
nodes.label: cor:explicitExprK_Z

nodes.name: Covariance of Z
nodes.statement: &{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)={\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)+{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}(u_1,u_2)\nonumber\\ &=\Mv{p}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}} + \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}} + \beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}.
nodes.label: eq:covZ_full

nodes.name: Matrix-valued metric D as pseudo-variogram of Z
nodes.statement: To do so, we let $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G \times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p \times p}$ be the pseudo-variogram of $\rVec{Z}$, \textit{i.e. } \begin{equation} \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2):=\grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)=\square{\mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(u_1)-Z_j(u_2)}}_{i,j=1}^p. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Distance as pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2):=\grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)=\square{\mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(u_1)-Z_j(u_2)}}_{i,j=1}^p.
nodes.label: eq:definitionOfDistance

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6 (sketch)
nodes.statement: A straightforward application of Equation (\ref{eq:pseudoVariogramMatricial}) in concert with tedious calculations provides the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the matrix form of the pseudo-variogram to the covariance of Z and compute.

nodes.name: Explicit form of the multivariate metric
nodes.statement: It is true that \begin{align} \latMatr{D}(u_1,&u_2)=\Mv{p}{\round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}} + \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}-2\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}\nonumber\\ &+\Mv{p}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\mathbbm{1} \round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2} \ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}, \end{align} for $u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal G$, with notation as in Proposition \ref{prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE}.
assumptions: for $u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal G$, with notation as in Proposition \ref{prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE}.
nodes.statement_short: D(u1,u2) is the sum of a Z_V block term in Sigma~, X~ and a Z_E block term in edge lengths and positions.
nodes.label: prop:explicitWritingMultivMetric

nodes.name: Explicit multivariate metric
nodes.statement: \latMatr{D}(u_1,&u_2)=\Mv{p}{\round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}} + \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}-2\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}\nonumber\\ &+\Mv{p}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\mathbbm{1} \round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2} \ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}},
nodes.label: eq:explicitWritingMultivMetric

nodes.name: Quasi-metric properties of D
nodes.statement: The matrix-valued expression (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}) satisfies properties similar to the (real-valued) quasi-metrics, \textit{i.e. } it satisfies: \begin{enumerate} \item $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)\geq 0$; \item $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)=0 \iff u_1=u_2$ and $i=j$; \item $\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2) = \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)^\top = \latMatr{D}(u_2,u_1) = \latMatr{D}(u_2,u_1)^\top$ for any $u_1, u_2 \in \mathcal G$; \item The mapping $(u_1,u_2) \mapsto \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_0) \latMatr{A} + \latMatr{A}^\top \latMatr{D}(u_0,u_2) - \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2) - \latMatr{A}^\top \latMatr{D}(u_0,u_0) \latMatr{A}$ is positive semidefinite for any $u_0 \in \mathcal G$ and any $p\times p$ matrix $\latMatr{A}$ such that $\latMatr{A}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{p}} = {\mathbf{1}_{p}}$; \item {The matrices $\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)-\latMatr{D}(u_0,u_0)$ and $2\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_0)+2\latMatr{D}(u_2,u_0)-\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)-3\latMatr{D}(u_0,u_0)$ are symmetric and positive semidefinite for any $u_0,u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal G$.} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: D is nonnegative, vanishes only on the diagonal at coincident points, is symmetric, and satisfies two semidefiniteness inequalities.
nodes.label: prop:actuallyQuasiMetricSpace

nodes.name: Marginals are resistance distances; D is matrix-homogeneous
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges and let $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G\times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}$ as defined in (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}) and having elements $D_{ij}$, $i,j=1,\ldots, p$. Then, the following properties hold: \begin{enumerate} \item for all $i\in\curly{1,\dots,p}$, the distance $D_{ii}$ coincides with the resistance distance defined by \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}, \textit{i.e. } $D_{ii}(u_1,u_2)=d_{R}(u_1,u_2)$; \item the distance $\latMatr{D}$ is matrix-homogeneous, \textit{i.e. } for every $ i\ne j$ and $\,i'\ne j'$, we have $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)=D_{i'j'}(u_1,u_2)$ and $D_{ii}(u_1,u_2)=D_{i'i'}(u_1,u_2)$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges
let $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G\times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}$ as defined in (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}) and having elements $D_{ij}$, $i,j=1,\ldots, p$.
nodes.statement_short: Each diagonal entry of D is the resistance metric, and all off-diagonal (and all diagonal) entries coincide.
nodes.label: prop:ourDistProperties

nodes.name: Within-variable distance need not be smaller than cross-variable distance
nodes.statement: Albeit counter-intuitive, the distance within the same variable is not always less than the same distance among variables. In formulae, $D_{ii}(u_1,u_2)\not\leq D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)$, in general.

nodes.name: Asymptotic properties of the metric
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges and let $\latMatr{Q}$ and ${\latMatr{X}}$ as defined in Equations (\ref{eq:defQ})-(\ref{eq:defXEigen}). Then, the asymptotic results {indicated in Table \ref{tab:asympt}} hold.\par \begin{table} \caption{Asymptotic results with respect to $p$ and $\alpha$. In the $4^\text{th}$ row, $0<\tau \leq \lambda_{n-1}$, with $\lambda_{n-1}$ being the smallest positive eigenvalue of $\grMatr{\Sigma}$, while in the last row, $\tau \geq \lambda_1$. In the last column, the results involving $d_R(u_1,u_2)$ hold only for $\beta \to 1$ (the other result holds for every $\beta\in[0,1]$). \tobi{Emilio, per essere formali qui dovremmo modificare le prime due righe della colonna Q e metterci il limite: sei d'accordo o lasciamo così?}} \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline $p$ & $\alpha$ & $\latMatr{Q}$ & ${\latMatr{X}}$ & $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)$ for $i\ne j$\\ \hline $+\infty$ & fixed & $\alpha(p-1){\latMatr{I}_n}$ & ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}$ & $d_R(u_1,u_2)$ \\ fixed & $+\infty$ & $\alpha(p-1){\latMatr{I}_n}$ & ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}$ & $d_R(u_1,u_2)$ \\ fixed & $0^+$ & ${\latMatr{L}}$ & $-\frac{1}{\alpha n (p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ & $\frac{2}{\alpha n p}$\\ $+\infty$ & $\frac{1}{p\tau}$ & $\frac{\latMatr I_n}{\tau}$ & $\grMatr{\Sigma} - \tau \latMatr I_n$ & $d_R(u_1,u_2) + 2\tau \dVec \delta_{1,V}^\top \dVec \delta_{2,V}$\\ $+\infty$ & $\frac{1}{p\tau}$ & $\latMatr L + \frac{1}{n\tau} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} $ & $-\frac{\tau}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} $ & $d_R(u_1,u_2)+\frac{2\tau}{n} + 2\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}^\top \latMatr X \dVec{\delta}_{2,V}$\\ \hline \end{tabular} \end{center} \end{table}
assumptions: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges
let $\latMatr{Q}$ and ${\latMatr{X}}$ as defined in Equations (\ref{eq:defQ})-(\ref{eq:defXEigen}).
conclusions: the asymptotic results {indicated in Table \ref{tab:asympt}} hold.
nodes.statement_short: Limits of Q, X and the cross distances D_ij as p or alpha tend to infinity or zero, listed in Table 1.
nodes.label: prop:asymptoticResults

nodes.name: Valid covariance functions from the multivariate metric
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges and $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G\times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}$ the distance defined at (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}). In addition, let $\psi:[0,+\infty)\to (0,+\infty)$ be a non-constant completely monotone function and $g: [0,+\infty)\to [0,+\infty)$ a Bernstein function. Then, for every $ {\xi}>0$, the mapping {$\latMatr{K}$ defined as} \begin{equation} (u_1,u_2)\mapsto {\latMatr{K}(u_1,u_2)} = \psi\round{ {\xi}\,g\round{\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)}}, \end{equation} where $\psi$ and $g$ are applied element-wise, is a valid covariance function. If, in addition, $\psi(0)=1$, then (\ref{eq:validCovarianceFunction}) is a valid correlation function.
assumptions: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges and $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G\times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}$ the distance defined at (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}).
let $\psi:[0,+\infty)\to (0,+\infty)$ be a non-constant completely monotone function
$g: [0,+\infty)\to [0,+\infty)$ a Bernstein function
If, in addition, $\psi(0)=1$
conclusions: then (\ref{eq:validCovarianceFunction}) is a valid correlation function.

assumptions: let $\psi:[0,+\infty)\to (0,+\infty)$ be a non-constant completely monotone function
$g: [0,+\infty)\to [0,+\infty)$ a Bernstein function
If, in addition, $\psi(0)=1$
conclusions: then (\ref{eq:validCovarianceFunction}) is a valid correlation function.

nodes.statement_short: psi(xi g(D)) applied element-wise is a valid matrix covariance (correlation if psi(0)=1) on any graph with Euclidean edges.
nodes.label: theo:covFunctionBuilding

nodes.name: Covariance from completely monotone and Bernstein functions
nodes.statement: (u_1,u_2)\mapsto {\latMatr{K}(u_1,u_2)} = \psi\round{ {\xi}\,g\round{\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)}},
nodes.label: eq:validCovarianceFunction

nodes.name: Homogeneity drawback of the construction
nodes.statement: One of the main drawbacks of this construction is that the distance is homogeneous (see Proposition \ref{prop:ourDistProperties}). Consequently, {not only do} the resulting {matrix-valued covariance function (\ref{eq:validCovarianceFunction}) assigns the same marginal covariance for all the variables, \textit{i.e. } $\psi( {\xi} g( {D_{ii}}(u_1,u_2))) = \psi( {\xi} g( {d_R}(u_1,u_2)))$ for any $u_1, u_2\in \mathcal G$ and any $i \in \{1,\ldots,p\}$}, {but also the cross-covariance between two different variables is independent from the variables themselves, \textit{i.e. } $\psi(\xi\, g(D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)))$ does not depend on $i,j$ as long as $i\ne j$.}
nodes.statement_short: Since D is homogeneous, all marginal covariances coincide and all cross-covariances coincide.

nodes.name: Rescaling by a correlation matrix preserves positive semidefiniteness
nodes.statement: Let $[\rho_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^p$ be a collocated correlation matrix, {\em e.g.}, $\rho_{ii}=1$ and $-1\leq \rho_{ij } \le 1$ when $i \ne j$, and the matrix being symmetric and positive semidefinite. Let $\dVec{\sigma} = (\sigma_1 ,\ldots, \sigma_p )^{\top}$ with $\sigma_i>0$ for $i=1,\ldots,p$. Let ${\latMatr{K}}$ be the mapping in (\ref{eq:validCovarianceFunction}) and define the mapping $\widetilde{{\latMatr{K}}} : \mathcal G \times \mathcal G \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ with entries $$ \widetilde{{{K}}}_{ij}(u_1,u_2) := \sigma_i \sigma_j \rho_{ij} {{K}}_{ij}(u_1,u_2), \quad i, j = 1,\ldots,p, \quad u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal G. $$ Then, by straight application of the Schur product theorem, one gets that $\widetilde{{\latMatr{K}}}$ is a positive semidefinite matrix-valued function.
assumptions: Let $[\rho_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^p$ be a collocated correlation matrix
Let $\dVec{\sigma} = (\sigma_1 ,\ldots, \sigma_p )^{\top}$ with $\sigma_i>0$ for $i=1,\ldots,p$.
Let ${\latMatr{K}}$ be the mapping in (\ref{eq:validCovarianceFunction})
conclusions: $\widetilde{{\latMatr{K}}}$ is a positive semidefinite matrix-valued function.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying K entrywise by sigma_i sigma_j rho_ij keeps it positive semidefinite (Schur product theorem).
