nodes.name: Embedding of Euclidean trees in l1 space
nodes.statement: Euclidean trees with a number $m$ of leaves can be embedded on the $m^\prime$-dimensional Euclidean space {with $m^\prime:=\lceil m/2 \rceil$} \citep{anderes_isotropic_2020} endowed with the $\ell_1$ distance: for a positive integer ${m^\prime}$ and two points $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}}$, the $\ell_1$ or Manhattan-city block distance $d_{M}$ can be defined as $d_{M}(x,y) = \sum_{k=1}^{{m^\prime}} |x_k-y_k|$.
conclusions: Euclidean trees with a number $m$ of leaves can be embedded on the $m^\prime$-dimensional Euclidean space {with $m^\prime:=\lceil m/2 \rceil$}
nodes.statement_short: A Euclidean tree with m leaves embeds isometrically into R^{ceil(m/2)} with the Manhattan (l1) distance d_M.

nodes.name: Class Phi_m^p
nodes.statement: Call $\Phi_{m}^p$ the class of continuous mappings ${\mathbf{K}}: [0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ such that the composition ${\mathbf{K}}(d_{M}(\cdot,\cdot))$ is positive {semi}definite on a Euclidean tree with $m$ leaves.

nodes.name: Schoenberg-type characterisation of the class Phi_m^p
nodes.statement: Let $m,p$ be two positive integers. {Let $m^\prime:=\lceil m/2 \rceil$.} Let ${\latMatr{K}}: [0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ be continuous with ${\latMatr{K}}(0)= \mathbf{1}_{p \times p}$. Then, ${\latMatr{K}}$ belongs to the class $\Phi_m^p$ if and only if \begin{equation} {\latMatr{K}}(t) = \int_0^{+\infty} \omega_{{m^\prime}} (rt ) \,{\latMatr{F}}({\rm d}r), \qquad t \ge 0, \end{equation} where ${\latMatr{F}}$ is a {bounded} {symmetric} matrix-valued measure such that ${\mathbf{F}} ({\rm d}r)$ is positive {semi}definite for all $r >0$, and where \begin{equation} \omega_{{m^\prime}}(t) = \frac{\Gamma({m^\prime}/2)}{\sqrt{\pi} \Gamma(({m^\prime}-1)/2)} \int_{1}^{+\infty} \Omega_{{m^\prime}} (\sqrt{v}t) v^{-{m^\prime}/2} (v-1)^{({m^\prime}-3)/2} {\rm d} v, \end{equation} with $\Omega_{{m^\prime}}$ being the characteristic function of a random vector that is uniformly distributed over the {unit sphere} $\mathbb{S}^{{m^\prime}-1}$ embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}}$.
assumptions: Let $m,p$ be two positive integers.
Let ${\latMatr{K}}: [0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ be continuous with ${\latMatr{K}}(0)= \mathbf{1}_{p \times p}$.
conclusions: ${\latMatr{K}}$ belongs to the class $\Phi_m^p$ if and only if
equivalent_conditions: where ${\latMatr{F}}$ is a {bounded} {symmetric} matrix-valued measure such that ${\mathbf{F}} ({\rm d}r)$ is positive {semi}definite for all $r >0$
nodes.statement_short: K is in Phi_m^p iff it is a scale mixture of the kernel omega_{m'} against a bounded psd matrix-valued measure.
nodes.label: prop:p-Schoen

nodes.label: eq:alpha-1

nodes.name: Kernel omega_{m'}
nodes.statement: \omega_{{m^\prime}}(t) = \frac{\Gamma({m^\prime}/2)}{\sqrt{\pi} \Gamma(({m^\prime}-1)/2)} \int_{1}^{+\infty} \Omega_{{m^\prime}} (\sqrt{v}t) v^{-{m^\prime}/2} (v-1)^{({m^\prime}-3)/2} {\rm d} v,

nodes.name: Strict nesting of the classes Phi_m^p
nodes.statement: The following strict inclusion relations hold: $$ \Phi_{1}^p \supset \Phi_2^p \supset \cdots \supset \bigcap_{m} \Phi_m^p =: \Phi_{\infty}^p. $$

nodes.name: Characterisation of Phi_infinity^p
nodes.statement: A convergence argument from \cite{schoenberg} applies \emph{mutatis mutandis} to assert (no proof needed) that ${\mathbf{K}} \in \Phi_{\infty}^p$ if and only if \begin{equation} {\mathbf{K}}(t) = \int_0^{+\infty} \exp(-rt) {\mathbf{F}}({\rm d}r), \qquad t \ge 0, \end{equation} with ${\mathbf{F}}$ as in Proposition \ref{prop:p-Schoen}.
nodes.statement_short: K is in Phi_infinity^p iff it is a mixture of exponentials exp(-rt) against a psd matrix measure.

nodes.name: Exponential-mixture representation
nodes.statement: {\mathbf{K}}(t) = \int_0^{+\infty} \exp(-rt) {\mathbf{F}}({\rm d}r), \qquad t \ge 0,
nodes.label: eq:alpha-2

nodes.name: Closed forms of omega_2 and omega_3
nodes.statement: Closed-form expressions for the inner kernel $\omega_{{m^\prime}}$ have been available thanks to \cite{gneiting1998onalpha}. In particular, we have \begin{equation*} \omega_2(t) = - \frac{2}{\pi} {\rm si}(t) \quad \text{and} \quad \omega_3(t) = \frac{1}{2} \Bigg ( \frac{\sin t}{t} + \cos t + t \; {\rm si}(t) \Bigg ), \quad t \ge 0, \end{equation*} where ${\rm si}$ denotes the sine integral function.

nodes.name: Class Psi_m^p
nodes.statement: There exists a wealth of multivariate covariance models that depend on the Euclidean distance, denoted $\|\cdot\|_{m}$, in $\mathbb{R}^m$. Call $\Psi_m^p$ the class of {continuous} mappings $\latMatr H: [0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ with $\latMatr H(0)= {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}$ and $\latMatr H(\|\cdot\|_m)$ being positive {semi}definite in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

nodes.name: Montee construction of members of Phi_m^p
nodes.statement: Let $m,p$ be positive integers. {Let $m^\prime:=\lceil m/2 \rceil$.} Let $\latMatr H$ be a member of the class $\Psi_{2{m^\prime}-1}^p$. Let the mapping ${\latMatr{K}}$ be defined through \begin{equation} {\latMatr{K}}(t) = I^{({m^\prime}-1)} \latMatr H(t), \qquad t \ge 0, \end{equation} where $I^{({m^\prime}-1)}$ is the $({m^\prime}-1)$ iterated application of the operator $I$, defined as \begin{equation*} (If)(t) := \frac{\int_{t}^{+\infty} f(u) {\rm d} u}{\int_{0}^{+\infty} f(u) {\rm d} u}. \end{equation*} Then, ${\mathbf{K}}$ belongs to the class $\Phi_m^p$.
assumptions: Let $m,p$ be positive integers.
Let $\latMatr H$ be a member of the class $\Psi_{2{m^\prime}-1}^p$.
nodes.statement_short: Applying the integral operator I (m'-1) times to a member of Psi_{2m'-1}^p yields a member of Phi_m^p.

nodes.name: Direct construction from the kernel omega
assumptions: Let $m,p$ be positive integers.
Let $[\rho_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^p$, $[b_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^p$ and $[\nu_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^p$ be real symmetric matrices such that $b_{ij}>0$ and $\nu_{ij}>2{m^\prime}-1$ for $i,j=1,\ldots,p$.
provided the matrix $\latMatr{A}(r)$ as defined in (\ref{eq:AA}) is positive semidefinite for any $r > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaled omega kernels K_ij = rho_ij b_ij^{-(2m'-1)} omega(x/b_ij) lie in Phi_m^p when the matrices A(r) are psd.
nodes.label: prop:infarto_miocardio

nodes.name: Matrix A(r)
nodes.label: eq:AA

nodes.name: Omega-based kernel
nodes.statement: K_{ij}(x) = \frac{\rho_{ij}}{b_{ij}^{{2{m^\prime}-1}}} \, \omega_{\nu_{ij}} \left ( \frac{x}{b_{ij}}\right ), \qquad x\ge 0, \quad i,j=1,\ldots, p,
nodes.label: eq:Omega-d

nodes.name: Bivariate Askey-type covariance on a tree with four leaves
nodes.statement: We conclude this section with an illustration to the bivariate setting ($p=2$) for a Euclidean tree with $m=4$ leaves. The entries of the covariance function are given by $K_{11}(d_R(u,v)) = (1- d_R(u,v)/4)_+^3$, $K_{22}(d_R(u,v)) = (1- d_R(u,v))_+^3$, and $K_{12}(d_R(u,v)) = 0.6 \times (1- d_R(u,v)/2.5)_+^3$, for all $u,v\in\mathcal{G}$. Here, the collocated correlation coefficient between the two random field components is $0.6$.

nodes.name: Product of M_p block matrices
nodes.statement: Let ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}},{\latMatr{C}},{\latMatr{D}}$ be $n \times n$ matrices and let $p\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$. Then \begin{equation} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}} = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}. \end{equation}
assumptions: Let ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}},{\latMatr{C}},{\latMatr{D}}$ be $n \times n$ matrices and let $p\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$.
nodes.statement_short: M_p(A,B) M_p(C,D) = M_p(AC+(p-1)BD, AD+BC+(p-2)BD).
nodes.label: lem:MpMp_expr

nodes.name: Product formula for M_p
nodes.statement: \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}} = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.1
nodes.statement: By the standard properties of the Kronecker product, \begin{align*} &\round{\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}}}\round{\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{C}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{D}}} = \\ & = (\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}}) (\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{C}}) + (\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}}) \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{D}}} \\ &\quad + \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}}} \round{\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{C}}} + \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}}} \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{D}}} \\ &= (\latMatr{I}_p \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}) + (\latMatr{I}_p({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p))\otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}) \\ &\quad + (({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}) + (({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p)({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p)) \otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}})\\ &= \latMatr{I}_p \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}})+({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}) + (p {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - 2\cdot {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}+\latMatr{I}_p)\otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}})\\ &=\latMatr{I}_p \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}) + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}})\\ &\quad + \big((p-2)({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) + (p-1) \latMatr{I}_p\big) \otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}) \\ &= \latMatr{I}_p \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}} + (p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}) + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the Kronecker-product representation and collect terms.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Throughout this proof, we assume that $\latMatr{L}\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, ${\latMatr{A}}\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_1}$ and ${\latMatr{C}}\in \mathbb{R}^{n_2 \times n_2}$, with $n_1,n_2>0$ and $n=n_1+n_2$.\par \begin{enumerate} \item Assume ${\latMatr{B}}=0$. Then $n-1 = \mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{L}})=\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{A}})+\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{C}})$. But since $\latMatr L {\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0$, it follows that ${\latMatr{A}} \dVec {1}_{n_1}=\dVec 0$ and ${\latMatr{C}} \dVec 1_{n_2}= \dVec0$. This implies that $\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{A}})\leq n_1-1$ and $\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{C}})\leq n_2 -1$. Contradiction. \item We will show only that ${\latMatr{C}}$ strictly positive definite, as the proof for the other case relies on the same argument. Since $\latMatr C$ is a principal submatrix of $\latMatr L$, it is positive semidefinite. As a consequence, it is sufficient to show that it is invertible. Assume, by contradiction, that ${\latMatr{C}}$ is singular. This is equivalent to assume that $\exists \dVec y\ne \dVec 0$ such that ${\latMatr{C}} \dVec y=\dVec 0$. Since $\latMatr L$ is positive semidefinite we have, for each $\dVec x\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1}$ and for each $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$: \begin{align*} 0 &\leq \begin{bmatrix} \dVec x \\ \gamma \dVec y \end{bmatrix}^\top \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}}^\top & {\latMatr{C}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dVec x \\ \gamma \dVec y \end{bmatrix}\\ &=\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{A}} \dVec x + \dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} (\gamma \dVec y) + (\gamma \dVec y)^\top {\latMatr{B}}^\top \dVec x + (\gamma \dVec y)^\top {\latMatr{C}} (\gamma \dVec y)=\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{A}} \dVec x + 2 \gamma \dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} \dVec y. \end{align*} If $\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} \dVec y\ne 0$, we can find a suitable $\gamma$ that contradicts the previous inequality. Hence $\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} \dVec y=0$ and therefore, being $\dVec x$ arbitrary, ${\latMatr{B}} \dVec y=\dVec 0$. Consider now the vector $\dVec z:=(0,...,0,\dVec y^\top)^\top$: we have ${\latMatr{L}}\dVec z=\dVec 0$, but clearly $\dVec z$ does not lie in the null space of $\latMatr L$, which is $\curly{\lambda {\mathbf{1}_{n}}\,:\,\lambda\in \mathbb{R}}$. Contradiction. \item Clearly ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}$ is symmetric. Furthermore, the Guttman rank additivity formula \cite[Equation 0.9.2]{zhang_schur_2005} states that $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}})=\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{C}}) + \mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}})$. Here we have $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}})=n-1$ and $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{C}})=n_2$, as a consequence $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}})=n_1-1$. Furthermore, from \citet[Theorem 1.12]{zhang_schur_2005}, being ${\latMatr{C}}$ strictly positive definite and $L$ positive semidefinite, we have that ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}$ is positive semidefinite as well. The last thing that is left to be shown is that the null eigenvector of ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}$ is ${\dVec 1}_{n_1}$. Since ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$ is the null eigenvector of $\latMatr L$, we get \begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}} \end{bmatrix}{\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0 \qquad \text{ and }\qquad \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{B}}^\top & {\latMatr{C}} \end{bmatrix}{\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0, \end{equation*} videlicet ${\latMatr{A}} \dVec{1}_{n_1}+{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}=\dVec 0$ and ${\latMatr{B}}^\top \dVec{1}_{n_1}+{\latMatr{C}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}=\dVec 0$. Using these relations, the following chain of equivalences concludes the proof: \begin{align*} &({\latMatr{A}}-{\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}^\top) \mathbf{1}_{n_1}= \dVec 0 \iff {\latMatr{A}} \mathbf{1}_{n_1} = {\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}^\top \dVec{1}_{n_1}\\ & \iff -{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}={\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1}(-{\latMatr{C}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}) \iff -{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2} = -{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}. \end{align*} \item Consider the eigendecomposition of $\latMatr L$: \begin{equation} {\latMatr{L}}=\latMatr W \begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \latMatr W^\top, \end{equation} with $\grMatr{\Delta}$ a $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ diagonal matrix with positive diagonal entries. Since $\latMatr W$ is an orthogonal matrix, we have \begin{equation} \begin{split} {\latMatr{L}}^-&=\round{\latMatr W \begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \latMatr W^\top}^-=(\latMatr W^\top)^-\begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^- \latMatr W^-=\latMatr W\begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta}^{-1} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \latMatr W^\top. \end{split} \end{equation} Therefore ${\latMatr{L}}^-$ is symmetric, is positive semidefinite and with exactly one null eigenvalue, corresponding to the same null-space eigenvector of $\latMatr L$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Rank counting and contradiction for parts 1-2; Guttman rank additivity for Schur complements; eigendecomposition for the pseudo-inverse.

nodes.name: Schur complement quasi-Laplacian via Guttman rank additivity

Furthermore, the Guttman rank additivity formula \cite[Equation 0.9.2]{zhang_schur_2005} states that $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}})=\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{C}}) + \mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}})$. Here we have $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}})=n-1$ and $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{C}})=n_2$, as a consequence $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}})=n_1-1$. The last thing that is left to be shown is that the null eigenvector of ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}$ is ${\dVec 1}_{n_1}$. Since ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$ is the null eigenvector of $\latMatr L$, we get \begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}} \end{bmatrix}{\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0 \qquad \text{ and }\qquad \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{B}}^\top & {\latMatr{C}} \end{bmatrix}{\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0, \end{equation*} videlicet ${\latMatr{A}} \dVec{1}_{n_1}+{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}=\dVec 0$ and ${\latMatr{B}}^\top \dVec{1}_{n_1}+{\latMatr{C}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}=\dVec 0$. nodes.name: Eigenvalues of Q
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr L$ be an $n \times n$ quasi-Laplacian matrix and ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}={\latMatr{L}}^-$. Let ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} =: \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \latMatr W^\top$ be the eigendecomposition of ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}$, with $\grMatr{\Lambda} = \mathrm{diag}\round{ \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n \end{bmatrix} }$ and $\lambda_1\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{n-1}>\lambda_n=0$. Let $\latMatr Q$ be defined as in Subsection \ref{ssec:constructionZ_V}. Then, the eigenvalues $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)<\lambda_1(\latMatr Q)\leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}(\latMatr Q)$ of $\latMatr Q$ are: \begin{equation*} \lambda_i(\latMatr Q) = \begin{dcases} \frac{1}{2} \round{\lambda_i^{-1}+\sqrt{\lambda_i^{-2}-2\alpha(p-2)\lambda_i^{-1}+\alpha^2 p^2}+\alpha(p-2)}\qquad &i\ne n\\ \alpha(p-1)\qquad &\text{$i=n$}. \end{dcases} \end{equation*} In particular the smallest eigenvalue of $\latMatr Q$, $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)$, is strictly positive, thus $\latMatr Q$ is strictly positive definite. In addition, $\latMatr Q {\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\alpha(p-1){\mathbf{1}_{n}}$.
assumptions: Let $\latMatr L$ be an $n \times n$ quasi-Laplacian matrix and ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}={\latMatr{L}}^-$.
Let $\latMatr Q$ be defined as in Subsection \ref{ssec:constructionZ_V}.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit eigenvalues of Q in terms of those of Sigma; Q is positive definite and Q 1 = alpha(p-1) 1.
nodes.label: lem:eigenvaluesQ

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.2
nodes.statement: Recall the eigendecomposition of matrix $\latMatr Q$ given in Equation (\ref{eq:defQEigen}): it is clear that the eigenvalues of $\latMatr Q$ are the elements on the diagonal of the matrix \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2}\round{\grMatr{\Lambda}^-+\sqrt{(\grMatr{\Lambda}^{-})^2-2\alpha(p-2)\grMatr{\Lambda}^-+\alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n}+\alpha(p-2)\latMatr{I}_n}, \end{equation*} which are $\curly{f(\lambda^-)\;:\;\lambda\in \curly{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n}}$, where {$\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are the diagonal entries of $\grMatr{\Lambda}$ (positive, except for $\lambda_n$ that is null) and} \begin{equation*} f(\lambda^-):=\frac{1}{2}\round{\lambda^-+\sqrt{\round{\lambda^-}^2-2\alpha(p-2)\lambda^-+\alpha^2 p^2}+\alpha(p-2)}. \end{equation*} Here, we recall that, for a scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda^-:=\lambda^{-1}$ if $\lambda \ne 0$ and $\lambda^-:=0$ if $\lambda=0$. It is straightforward to show that $\lambda^- \mapsto f(\lambda^-)$ is a strictly increasing function on $\lambda^- \geq 0$. As a consequence, since $\lambda \mapsto \lambda^-$ is strictly decreasing on $\lambda > 0$, $\lambda \mapsto f(\lambda^-)$ is strictly decreasing on $\lambda>0$. Therefore, $\lambda_1\geq\dots\geq \lambda_{n-1}$ are mapped in $\lambda_1(\latMatr Q)=f(\lambda_1^{-1})\leq\dots\leq \lambda_{n-1}(\latMatr Q)= f(\lambda_{n-1}^{-1})$. For the case $\lambda_n=0$, we have $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)=f(\lambda_n^-)=f(0)=\frac{1}{2}\round{\alpha p + \alpha(p-2)}=\alpha(p-1)$. In addition, since $\lambda_n=0<\lambda_1(\latMatr Q)$, we have $\alpha(p-1) = \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) < \lambda_1(\latMatr Q)$. \\ Finally, to show that $\latMatr Q {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \alpha(p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, it is sufficient to notice from the eigendecomposition of $\latMatr Q$ given in Equation (\ref{eq:defQEigen}) that ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, being (proportional to) the last column of $\latMatr W$, is an eigenvector of $\latMatr Q$. And by the above result it is clear that the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)=\alpha(p-1)$. This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Read eigenvalues off the spectral form of Q and use monotonicity of the scalar map f.

nodes.name: Eigenvalues of Q as f(lambda^-); f increasing
nodes.statement: Recall the eigendecomposition of matrix $\latMatr Q$ given in Equation (\ref{eq:defQEigen}): it is clear that the eigenvalues of $\latMatr Q$ are the elements on the diagonal of the matrix \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2}\round{\grMatr{\Lambda}^-+\sqrt{(\grMatr{\Lambda}^{-})^2-2\alpha(p-2)\grMatr{\Lambda}^-+\alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n}+\alpha(p-2)\latMatr{I}_n}, \end{equation*} which are $\curly{f(\lambda^-)\;:\;\lambda\in \curly{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n}}$, where {$\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are the diagonal entries of $\grMatr{\Lambda}$ (positive, except for $\lambda_n$ that is null) and} \begin{equation*} f(\lambda^-):=\frac{1}{2}\round{\lambda^-+\sqrt{\round{\lambda^-}^2-2\alpha(p-2)\lambda^-+\alpha^2 p^2}+\alpha(p-2)}. \end{equation*} Here, we recall that, for a scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda^-:=\lambda^{-1}$ if $\lambda \ne 0$ and $\lambda^-:=0$ if $\lambda=0$. It is straightforward to show that $\lambda^- \mapsto f(\lambda^-)$ is a strictly increasing function on $\lambda^- \geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Eigenvalues of Q as f(lambda^-); f increasing

nodes.name: Order of eigenvalues of Q
nodes.statement: As a consequence, since $\lambda \mapsto \lambda^-$ is strictly decreasing on $\lambda > 0$, $\lambda \mapsto f(\lambda^-)$ is strictly decreasing on $\lambda>0$. Therefore, $\lambda_1\geq\dots\geq \lambda_{n-1}$ are mapped in $\lambda_1(\latMatr Q)=f(\lambda_1^{-1})\leq\dots\leq \lambda_{n-1}(\latMatr Q)= f(\lambda_{n-1}^{-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Order of eigenvalues of Q

nodes.name: Smallest eigenvalue alpha(p-1)
nodes.statement: For the case $\lambda_n=0$, we have $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)=f(\lambda_n^-)=f(0)=\frac{1}{2}\round{\alpha p + \alpha(p-2)}=\alpha(p-1)$. In addition, since $\lambda_n=0<\lambda_1(\latMatr Q)$, we have $\alpha(p-1) = \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) < \lambda_1(\latMatr Q)$. \\
nodes.statement_short: Smallest eigenvalue alpha(p-1)

nodes.name: 1_n is the eigenvector for alpha(p-1)
nodes.statement: Finally, to show that $\latMatr Q {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \alpha(p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, it is sufficient to notice from the eigendecomposition of $\latMatr Q$ given in Equation (\ref{eq:defQEigen}) that ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, being (proportional to) the last column of $\latMatr W$, is an eigenvector of $\latMatr Q$. And by the above result it is clear that the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)=\alpha(p-1)$. This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: 1_n is the eigenvector for alpha(p-1)

nodes.name: Useful identities for Sigma, L, Q, X
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr L$ be an $n \times n$ quasi-Laplacian matrix, ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}={\latMatr{L}}^-$ and $\alpha >0$. Furthermore, let $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr X$ as defined in Subsection \ref{ssec:constructionZ_V}. Then the following holds: \begin{enumerate} \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}$, $\latMatr L$, $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr X$ commute; \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= {\latMatr{L}}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} = \latMatr{I}_n-\frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$; \item $\latMatr Q^2-\alpha^2 (p-1) \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr Q {\latMatr{L}}- \alpha (p-2) \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}= \matr 0$; \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2 (p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q - \alpha (p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n + \frac{\alpha}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}=\matr 0$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $\latMatr L$ be an $n \times n$ quasi-Laplacian matrix,
${\grMatr{\Sigma}}={\latMatr{L}}^-$ and $\alpha >0$.
let $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr X$ as defined in Subsection \ref{ssec:constructionZ_V}.
nodes.statement_short: Sigma, L, Q, X commute; Sigma L = I - (1/n)1; Q satisfies a quadratic matrix equation, also after multiplying by Sigma.
nodes.label: lem:usefulIdentities

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.3
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item It is sufficient to notice that all the matrices share the same eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$, \textit{i.e. } for any ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}\in\curly{{\grMatr{\Sigma}},\latMatr L,\latMatr Q,\latMatr X}$, there are two diagonal matrices $\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}},\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}}$ such that ${\latMatr{A}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}}\matr W^\top$ and ${\latMatr{B}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top$. Therefore \begin{align*} {\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{B}}&=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top\\ &=\latMatr W\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top = {\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{A}}. \end{align*} \item By exploiting the diagonalisations ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \latMatr W^\top$ (Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}) and ${\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}^- \latMatr W^\top$ (Eqs. (\ref{eq:eigL1}) and (\ref{eq:eigL2})), we get: \begin{align*} {\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \grMatr{\Lambda}^- \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W (\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n) \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top. \end{align*} Given that $\latMatr L$ is a quasi-Laplacian matrix, its eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$ can be written as \begin{equation*} \latMatr W = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix}, \end{equation*} where $\latMatr U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (n-1)}$ and $n c^2=1$. Therefore \begin{align} \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \matr 0_{(n-1)\times(n-1)} & \matr 0_{(n-1)\times 1}\\ \matr 0_{1 \times (n-1)} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U^\top \\ c {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top \end{bmatrix}= \frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top, \end{align} and this concludes the proof. \item From the definition (\ref{eq:defQ}) of $\latMatr Q$, one has: \begin{equation*} 2\latMatr Q - {\latMatr{L}}- \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n = \sqrt{{\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n}. \end{equation*} Now, taking the square of both sides (recall that $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr L$ commute): \begin{align*} &4 \latMatr Q^2 + {\latMatr{L}}^2 + \alpha^2 (p-2)^2 \latMatr{I}_n - 4 \latMatr Q{\latMatr{L}}- 4 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr Q + 2 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr L\\ &= {\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n. \end{align*} By grouping the common terms and dividing everything by $4$ we get the desired result. \item To show the second assertion, it is sufficient to multiply the first equation by ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = {\latMatr{L}}^-$: \begin{align*} &{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2(p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q ({\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}) - \alpha(p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) ({\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}) = \matr 0\\ &{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2 (p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q + \frac{1}{n} \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha (p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n \\ &\quad - \frac{\alpha (p-2)}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}=\matr 0, \end{align*} where we have used ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ and $\latMatr Q {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}= \alpha(p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$ (Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Common eigenvectors give commutation; spectral computation of Sigma L; square the defining equation of Q.

nodes.name: Commutation via shared eigenvectors
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to notice that all the matrices share the same eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$, \textit{i.e. } for any ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}\in\curly{{\grMatr{\Sigma}},\latMatr L,\latMatr Q,\latMatr X}$, there are two diagonal matrices $\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}},\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}}$ such that ${\latMatr{A}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}}\matr W^\top$ and ${\latMatr{B}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top$. Therefore \begin{align*} {\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{B}}&=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top\\ &=\latMatr W\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top = {\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{A}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Commutation via shared eigenvectors

nodes.name: Sigma L = I - (1/n) 1
nodes.statement: By exploiting the diagonalisations ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \latMatr W^\top$ (Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}) and ${\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}^- \latMatr W^\top$ (Eqs. (\ref{eq:eigL1}) and (\ref{eq:eigL2})), we get: \begin{align*} {\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \grMatr{\Lambda}^- \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W (\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n) \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top. \end{align*} Given that $\latMatr L$ is a quasi-Laplacian matrix, its eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$ can be written as \begin{equation*} \latMatr W = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix}, \end{equation*} where $\latMatr U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (n-1)}$ and $n c^2=1$. Therefore \begin{align} \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \matr 0_{(n-1)\times(n-1)} & \matr 0_{(n-1)\times 1}\\ \matr 0_{1 \times (n-1)} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U^\top \\ c {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top \end{bmatrix}= \frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top, \end{align} and this concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Sigma L = I - (1/n) 1

nodes.name: W J_n W^T = (1/n) 1 1^T
nodes.statement: \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \matr 0_{(n-1)\times(n-1)} & \matr 0_{(n-1)\times 1}\\ \matr 0_{1 \times (n-1)} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U^\top \\ c {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top \end{bmatrix}= \frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top,
nodes.label: eq:WJWtop_expr

nodes.name: Square the defining equation of Q
nodes.statement: From the definition (\ref{eq:defQ}) of $\latMatr Q$, one has: \begin{equation*} 2\latMatr Q - {\latMatr{L}}- \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n = \sqrt{{\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n}. \end{equation*} Now, taking the square of both sides (recall that $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr L$ commute): \begin{align*} &4 \latMatr Q^2 + {\latMatr{L}}^2 + \alpha^2 (p-2)^2 \latMatr{I}_n - 4 \latMatr Q{\latMatr{L}}- 4 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr Q + 2 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr L\\ &= {\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n. \end{align*} By grouping the common terms and dividing everything by $4$ we get the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Square the defining equation of Q

nodes.name: Multiply by Sigma
nodes.statement: To show the second assertion, it is sufficient to multiply the first equation by ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = {\latMatr{L}}^-$: \begin{align*} &{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2(p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q ({\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}) - \alpha(p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) ({\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}) = \matr 0\\ &{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2 (p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q + \frac{1}{n} \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha (p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n \\ &\quad - \frac{\alpha (p-2)}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}=\matr 0, \end{align*} where we have used ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ and $\latMatr Q {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}= \alpha(p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$ (Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}).
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by Sigma

nodes.name: Sum of matrices with complementary eigenvalue bounds
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr X,\latMatr Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric matrices. For $i\in\curly{1,\dots,n}$, let $\lambda_i(\latMatr X)$ and $\lambda_i(\latMatr Y)$ denote the $i^\text{th}$ eigenvalues of $\latMatr X$ and $\latMatr Y$, respectively. Let $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\lambda_i(\latMatr X)\geq c$ and $\lambda_i(\latMatr Y)\geq -c$ for all $i\in\curly{1,\dots,n}$. Then $\latMatr X+\latMatr Y$ is positive semidefinite.
assumptions: Let $\latMatr X,\latMatr Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric matrices.
Let $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\lambda_i(\latMatr X)\geq c$ and $\lambda_i(\latMatr Y)\geq -c$ for all $i\in\curly{1,\dots,n}$.
conclusions: Then $\latMatr X+\latMatr Y$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.label: lem:sumOfMatricesPD

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr X=\latMatr W_1\grMatr{\Delta}_1 \latMatr W_1^\top$ and $\latMatr Y=\latMatr W_2\grMatr{\Delta}_2 \latMatr W_2^\top$ be the eigendecompositions of $\latMatr X$ and $\latMatr Y$ and let $\dVec v\in\mathbb{R}^n$. In the following lines, we have defined $\dVec a:=\latMatr W_1^\top \dVec v$ and $\dVec b:= \latMatr W_2^\top \dVec v$. \begin{align*} \dVec v^\top (\latMatr X+\latMatr Y) \dVec v&=\dVec v^\top \latMatr W_1 \Delta_1 \latMatr W_1^\top \dVec v +\dVec v \latMatr W_2 \grMatr{\Delta}_2 \latMatr W_2^\top\dVec v= \dVec a^\top \grMatr{\Delta}_1\dVec a +\dVec b^\top \grMatr{\Delta}_2\dVec b \\ & = \sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(\latMatr X) a_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i(\latMatr Y) b_i^2\geq c \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - c \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\\ &=c(\dVec a^\top \dVec a - \dVec b^\top \dVec b) = c(\dVec v^\top \dVec v-\dVec v^\top \dVec v)=0. \end{align*} Videlicet, $\latMatr X+\latMatr Y$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: Write the quadratic form in the two eigenbases and bound by c|v|^2 - c|v|^2 = 0.

nodes.name: K-tilde is the Moore-Penrose inverse of Theta
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr{L}$ an $n\times n$ Laplacian matrix, let ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}:={\latMatr{L}}^-$ its Moore-Penrose inverse and let $\alpha > 0$. Let $\grMatr{\Theta}$, $\latMatr Q$, $\latMatr X$, $k_1$, $k_2$, $\Tilde{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}$ and $\Tilde{\latMatr X}$ as described in Subsection \ref{ssec:constructionZ_V}. Finally let: \begin{equation} \Tilde {\latMatr K} := \Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde {\latMatr X}}. \end{equation} Then $\Tilde{\latMatr K}=\grMatr{\Theta}^-$.
assumptions: Let $\latMatr{L}$ an $n\times n$ Laplacian matrix, let ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}:={\latMatr{L}}^-$ its Moore-Penrose inverse and let $\alpha > 0$.
nodes.label: lem:KinverseTheta

nodes.name: Definition of K-tilde
nodes.statement: \Tilde {\latMatr K} := \Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde {\latMatr X}}.
nodes.label: eq:defKTilde

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.5
nodes.statement: In order to show that $\Tilde{\latMatr K} = \grMatr{\Theta}^-$, by definition of the Moore-Penrose inverse, we need to prove \begin{enumerate} \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}$ and $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}$ are symmetric, \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \grMatr{\Theta}$, \item $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}$. \end{enumerate} To show symmetry, recall from Lemma \ref{lem:usefulIdentities} that all the matrices $\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ commute. As a consequence, $\forall {\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}},{\latMatr{C}},{\latMatr{D}} \in \curly{\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}$, it holds (Lemma \ref{lem:MpMp_expr}): \begin{align*} &\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}} = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{A}}+(p-1){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}{{\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{A}}+{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{B}}+(p-2){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}. \end{align*} In addition, $\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}^\top=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}^\top}{{\latMatr{B}}^\top}=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}$, as ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}$ are symmetric. Therefore, \begin{align*} &\round{\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}}^\top = \Tilde{\latMatr K}^\top \grMatr{\Theta}^\top = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}^\top \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}^\top \\ &= \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}^\top + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}^\top}{\latMatr X^\top + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}^\top} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}^\top}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &=\Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} + \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} + \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}. \end{align*} The same arguments show that $\round{\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}}^\top = \Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}$. To prove the other two relations, we start with following equalities. In the next lines, we used Lemmas \ref{lem:MpMp_expr}, \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ} and \ref{lem:usefulIdentities}. \begin{align*} \allowdisplaybreaks &\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \alpha(p-1)\latMatr X}{{\latMatr Q}\latMatr X-\alpha {\grMatr{\Sigma}}-\alpha(p-2)\latMatr X}\\ &\quad=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\alpha(p-1)\frac{1}{-\alpha(p-1)}(\latMatr{I}_n-{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr Q})}{\frac{1}{-\alpha(p-1)}({\latMatr Q}-{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr Q}^2)-\alpha{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\alpha(p-2)\latMatr X}=\Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\alpha (p-1)\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n - \frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha(p-2)\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad =\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta}\, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Mv{p}{k_1 {\latMatr Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-\alpha (p-1) k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\latMatr Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha k_2 (p-2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad=\Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta}\, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1){\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha^2 (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\alpha^2(p-1)(k_2-k_1){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha(k_1-k_2){\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} +\alpha^2(p-2)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{\alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ \intertext{As a consequence:} &\grMatr{\Theta}\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \grMatr{\Theta} \round{\latMatr K+\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}} \grMatr{\Theta}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} + \Mv{p}{\alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} = \grMatr{\Theta}. \intertext{Similarly we prove that $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}$:} &\latMatr{K}\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} \Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\frac{1}{n} \latMatr X {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \latMatr X - \frac{p-2}{n(p-2)}\latMatr X {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + \frac{1}{\alpha n (p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X+\frac{p-2}{\alpha n (p-1)^2}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} }\\ &\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} = \latMatr{K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad =\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} -\frac{1}{n}k_2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\frac{k_1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}+k_2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} -\frac{k_2(p-2)}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\frac{1}{p-1}(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} }\\ &\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} =\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)k_1(k_2-k_1) n{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-(p-1)\alpha k_2(k_1-k_2)n{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\big(-\alpha k_1 (k_1-k_2) n - \alpha(p-1)k_2(k_2-k_1) n -\alpha(p-2)k_2(k_1-k_2) n\big) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{\alpha n(p-1)(k_1-k_2)^2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha n (k_1-k_2)^2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \intertext{Therefore,} &\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \latMatr K\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr K + 2 \, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr K + \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify the Moore-Penrose conditions using the M_p product formula and the commuting identities.

nodes.name: Reduce to the Moore-Penrose conditions
nodes.statement: In order to show that $\Tilde{\latMatr K} = \grMatr{\Theta}^-$, by definition of the Moore-Penrose inverse, we need to prove \begin{enumerate} \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}$ and $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}$ are symmetric, \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \grMatr{\Theta}$, \item $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the Moore-Penrose conditions

nodes.name: M_p blocks with commuting entries commute
nodes.statement: To show symmetry, recall from Lemma \ref{lem:usefulIdentities} that all the matrices $\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ commute. As a consequence, $\forall {\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}},{\latMatr{C}},{\latMatr{D}} \in \curly{\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}$, it holds (Lemma \ref{lem:MpMp_expr}): \begin{align*} &\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}} = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{A}}+(p-1){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}{{\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{A}}+{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{B}}+(p-2){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: M_p blocks with commuting entries commute

nodes.name: Symmetry of Theta K-tilde and K-tilde Theta
nodes.statement: In addition, $\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}^\top=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}^\top}{{\latMatr{B}}^\top}=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}$, as ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}$ are symmetric. Therefore, \begin{align*} &\round{\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}}^\top = \Tilde{\latMatr K}^\top \grMatr{\Theta}^\top = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}^\top \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}^\top \\ &= \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}^\top + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}^\top}{\latMatr X^\top + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}^\top} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}^\top}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &=\Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} + \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} + \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}. \end{align*} The same arguments show that $\round{\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}}^\top = \Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}$.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry of Theta K-tilde and K-tilde Theta

nodes.name: Verify Theta K Theta = Theta and K Theta K = K
nodes.statement: To prove the other two relations, we start with following equalities. In the next lines, we used Lemmas \ref{lem:MpMp_expr}, \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ} and \ref{lem:usefulIdentities}. \begin{align*} \allowdisplaybreaks &\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \alpha(p-1)\latMatr X}{{\latMatr Q}\latMatr X-\alpha {\grMatr{\Sigma}}-\alpha(p-2)\latMatr X}\\ &\quad=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\alpha(p-1)\frac{1}{-\alpha(p-1)}(\latMatr{I}_n-{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr Q})}{\frac{1}{-\alpha(p-1)}({\latMatr Q}-{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr Q}^2)-\alpha{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\alpha(p-2)\latMatr X}=\Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\alpha (p-1)\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n - \frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha(p-2)\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad =\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta}\, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Mv{p}{k_1 {\latMatr Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-\alpha (p-1) k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\latMatr Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha k_2 (p-2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad=\Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta}\, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1){\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha^2 (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\alpha^2(p-1)(k_2-k_1){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha(k_1-k_2){\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} +\alpha^2(p-2)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{\alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ \intertext{As a consequence:} &\grMatr{\Theta}\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \grMatr{\Theta} \round{\latMatr K+\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}} \grMatr{\Theta}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} + \Mv{p}{\alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} = \grMatr{\Theta}. \intertext{Similarly we prove that $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}$:} &\latMatr{K}\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} \Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\frac{1}{n} \latMatr X {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \latMatr X - \frac{p-2}{n(p-2)}\latMatr X {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + \frac{1}{\alpha n (p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X+\frac{p-2}{\alpha n (p-1)^2}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} }\\ &\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} = \latMatr{K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad =\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} -\frac{1}{n}k_2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\frac{k_1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}+k_2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} -\frac{k_2(p-2)}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\frac{1}{p-1}(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} }\\ &\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} =\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)k_1(k_2-k_1) n{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-(p-1)\alpha k_2(k_1-k_2)n{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\big(-\alpha k_1 (k_1-k_2) n - \alpha(p-1)k_2(k_2-k_1) n -\alpha(p-2)k_2(k_1-k_2) n\big) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{\alpha n(p-1)(k_1-k_2)^2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha n (k_1-k_2)^2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \intertext{Therefore,} &\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \latMatr K\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr K + 2 \, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr K + \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify Theta K Theta = Theta and K Theta K = K

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: We first show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is quasi-Laplacian. To this end, we need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric, positive semidefinite, $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np}=\dVec 0$, and $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has only one null eigenvalue. \begin{enumerate} \item Since $\latMatr{Q}$ and $\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ are symmetric and $\grMatr{\Theta}:=\Mh{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}$, $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric. \item First recall that $\grMatr{\Theta} = \matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) + {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$: we aim to apply Lemma \ref{lem:sumOfMatricesPD} to the matrix $\grMatr{\Theta}$ with $\latMatr X:=\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$ and $\latMatr Y:={\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$. In the following, we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})$ to denote the vector of eigenvalues of ${\latMatr{A}}$. In addition, the inequalities apply to all elements: we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$ as a shortcut of $\forall i\in\curly{1,\dots,n},\,\lambda_i({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$, for an $n\times n$ matrix ${\latMatr{A}}$. \begin{align*} \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{X}) &= \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) ={\mathbf{1}_{p}} \otimes (\dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}) + \alpha) \\ &\geq \lambda_n(\latMatr{Q}) +\alpha = \alpha (p-1) +\alpha = \alpha p\\ \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Y}) &= \dVec{\lambda}({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} \otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \begin{bmatrix} p\\ 0\\ \vdots\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\otimes \begin{bmatrix} -\alpha \\ \vdots \\ -\alpha \end{bmatrix}\geq -\alpha p. \end{align*} Therefore $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is positive semidefinite. \item To show $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np} = \dVec 0$, given the special structure of $\grMatr{\Theta}$, it is sufficient to show that \begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{1}_{np} = \dVec 0, \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. } $\latMatr{Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \alpha (p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, {which has already been proved in Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}}. \item We now need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has no other null eigenvalues, \textit{i.e. } the only solution to \begin{equation} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \latMatr{Q} & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & \latMatr{Q} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dVec v_1\\ \dVec v_2\\ \vdots\\ \dVec v_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dVec 0 \\ \dVec 0 \\ \vdots\\ \dVec 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{equation} is (up to a multiplicative constant) $\dVec v_1=\dots=\dVec v_n={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$. By reading Equation (\ref{eq:Theta_v_equal_0}) by blocks, we get the following: $\forall i \in \curly{1,\dots,n}$ \begin{align*} \latMatr{Q} \dVec v_i - \alpha \sum_{k\ne i} \dVec v_k = \dVec 0. \end{align*} Taking now the difference for $i=i$ and $i=j$, we get \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)(\dVec v_i-\dVec v_j)=\dVec 0 \end{equation*} and, since $\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ is strictly positive definite directly by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, we obtain that $\dVec v_i=\dVec v_j=:\dVec v$ for all $i,j$. The problem thus becomes \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1)\latMatr{I}_n) \dVec v = \dVec 0. \end{equation*} To conclude it is sufficient to notice that the eigenvalues of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1) \latMatr{I}_n$ are $\lambda_i(\latMatr{Q}) - \alpha (p-1)$ and, by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, all the eigenvalues are not less than $\alpha(p-1)$ and exactly one achieve such a value. As a consequence, the kernel of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n$ has dimension one and, since we already know that $(\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n){\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0$, the only possibility is $\dVec v={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$. \end{enumerate} That $\grMatr{\Theta}^-$ is also a quasi-Laplacian matrix comes from Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and the closure of the set of quasi-Laplacian matrices under Moore-Penrose inversion (Proposition \ref{prop:quasiLaplacianProperties}).
nodes.statement_short: Check symmetry, psd (via Lemma A.4), the null vector and its uniqueness; then pseudo-inverse via Lemma A.5 and Proposition 1.

nodes.name: List the quasi-Laplacian properties to check
nodes.statement: We first show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is quasi-Laplacian. To this end, we need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric, positive semidefinite, $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np}=\dVec 0$, and $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has only one null eigenvalue.
nodes.statement_short: List the quasi-Laplacian properties to check

nodes.name: Symmetry
nodes.statement: Since $\latMatr{Q}$ and $\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ are symmetric and $\grMatr{\Theta}:=\Mh{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}$, $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite via Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: First recall that $\grMatr{\Theta} = \matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) + {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$: we aim to apply Lemma \ref{lem:sumOfMatricesPD} to the matrix $\grMatr{\Theta}$ with $\latMatr X:=\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$ and $\latMatr Y:={\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$. In the following, we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})$ to denote the vector of eigenvalues of ${\latMatr{A}}$. In addition, the inequalities apply to all elements: we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$ as a shortcut of $\forall i\in\curly{1,\dots,n},\,\lambda_i({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$, for an $n\times n$ matrix ${\latMatr{A}}$. \begin{align*} \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{X}) &= \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) ={\mathbf{1}_{p}} \otimes (\dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}) + \alpha) \\ &\geq \lambda_n(\latMatr{Q}) +\alpha = \alpha (p-1) +\alpha = \alpha p\\ \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Y}) &= \dVec{\lambda}({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} \otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \begin{bmatrix} p\\ 0\\ \vdots\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\otimes \begin{bmatrix} -\alpha \\ \vdots \\ -\alpha \end{bmatrix}\geq -\alpha p. \end{align*} Therefore $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: Positive semidefinite via Lemma A.4

nodes.name: Theta 1 = 0 via Q 1 = alpha(p-1) 1
nodes.statement: To show $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np} = \dVec 0$, given the special structure of $\grMatr{\Theta}$, it is sufficient to show that \begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{1}_{np} = \dVec 0, \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. } $\latMatr{Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \alpha (p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, {which has already been proved in Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}}.
nodes.statement_short: Theta 1 = 0 via Q 1 = alpha(p-1) 1

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the null eigenvector
nodes.statement: We now need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has no other null eigenvalues, \textit{i.e. } the only solution to \begin{equation} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \latMatr{Q} & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & \latMatr{Q} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dVec v_1\\ \dVec v_2\\ \vdots\\ \dVec v_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dVec 0 \\ \dVec 0 \\ \vdots\\ \dVec 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{equation} is (up to a multiplicative constant) $\dVec v_1=\dots=\dVec v_n={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$. By reading Equation (\ref{eq:Theta_v_equal_0}) by blocks, we get the following: $\forall i \in \curly{1,\dots,n}$ \begin{align*} \latMatr{Q} \dVec v_i - \alpha \sum_{k\ne i} \dVec v_k = \dVec 0. \end{align*} Taking now the difference for $i=i$ and $i=j$, we get \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)(\dVec v_i-\dVec v_j)=\dVec 0 \end{equation*} and, since $\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ is strictly positive definite directly by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, we obtain that $\dVec v_i=\dVec v_j=:\dVec v$ for all $i,j$. The problem thus becomes \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1)\latMatr{I}_n) \dVec v = \dVec 0. \end{equation*} To conclude it is sufficient to notice that the eigenvalues of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1) \latMatr{I}_n$ are $\lambda_i(\latMatr{Q}) - \alpha (p-1)$ and, by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, all the eigenvalues are not less than $\alpha(p-1)$ and exactly one achieve such a value. As a consequence, the kernel of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n$ has dimension one and, since we already know that $(\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n){\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0$, the only possibility is $\dVec v={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of the null eigenvector

nodes.name: Null-space equation for Theta
nodes.statement: \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \latMatr{Q} & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & \latMatr{Q} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dVec v_1\\ \dVec v_2\\ \vdots\\ \dVec v_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dVec 0 \\ \dVec 0 \\ \vdots\\ \dVec 0 \end{bmatrix}
nodes.label: eq:Theta_v_equal_0

nodes.name: Theta^- quasi-Laplacian by Lemma A.5 and Proposition 1
nodes.statement: That $\grMatr{\Theta}^-$ is also a quasi-Laplacian matrix comes from Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and the closure of the set of quasi-Laplacian matrices under Moore-Penrose inversion (Proposition \ref{prop:quasiLaplacianProperties}).
nodes.statement_short: Theta^- quasi-Laplacian by Lemma A.5 and Proposition 1

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to apply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalentFormPositDef} with $X:=V$. We show that the $np\times np$ matrix $[\latMatr K(v_i,v_j)]_{i,j=1}^{np}$ is positive semidefinite. First, notice that $[\latMatr K(v_i,v_j)]_{i,j=1}^{np}=\Mh{p}{\Tilde{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde{\latMatr X}}=\Tilde{\latMatr K}$. Since $\Tilde{\latMatr K}\in \mathbb{R}^{np \times np}$ is positive semidefinite (see Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}), each matrix ${\latMatr{C}}$ as defined in Proposition \ref{prop:equivalentFormPositDef}, being a principal submatrix of $\matr {\Tilde{\latMatr K}}$, is positive semidefinite as well. This proves the Proposition.
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 2, reduce to psd of the block matrix K-tilde, which is the pseudo-inverse of the quasi-Laplacian Theta.

nodes.name: Reduce to Proposition 2 with X=V
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to apply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalentFormPositDef} with $X:=V$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Proposition 2 with X=V

nodes.name: Claim: the block matrix is psd
nodes.statement: We show that the $np\times np$ matrix $[\latMatr K(v_i,v_j)]_{i,j=1}^{np}$ is positive semidefinite. First, notice that $[\latMatr K(v_i,v_j)]_{i,j=1}^{np}=\Mh{p}{\Tilde{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde{\latMatr X}}=\Tilde{\latMatr K}$. Since $\Tilde{\latMatr K}\in \mathbb{R}^{np \times np}$ is positive semidefinite (see Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}), each matrix ${\latMatr{C}}$ as defined in Proposition \ref{prop:equivalentFormPositDef}, being a principal submatrix of $\matr {\Tilde{\latMatr K}}$, is positive semidefinite as well. This proves the Proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the block matrix is psd

nodes.name: The block matrix equals K-tilde
nodes.statement: First, notice that $[\latMatr K(v_i,v_j)]_{i,j=1}^{np}=\Mh{p}{\Tilde{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde{\latMatr X}}=\Tilde{\latMatr K}$.
nodes.statement_short: The block matrix equals K-tilde

nodes.name: K-tilde psd, principal submatrices psd
nodes.statement: Since $\Tilde{\latMatr K}\in \mathbb{R}^{np \times np}$ is positive semidefinite (see Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}), each matrix ${\latMatr{C}}$ as defined in Proposition \ref{prop:equivalentFormPositDef}, being a principal submatrix of $\matr {\Tilde{\latMatr K}}$, is positive semidefinite as well. This proves the Proposition.
nodes.statement_short: K-tilde psd, principal submatrices psd

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The proof of this point is straightforward, as the pseudo variogram only takes non-negative values. \item {The condition $u_1 = u_2$ and $i=j$ is sufficient to have $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)=0$ due to the fact that the diagonal entries of $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_1,u_1)$ are zero. Let us show that it is also necessary. From the definition of the pseudo-variogram as per Equation (\ref{eq:pseudoVariogramDef}), $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2) = 0$ if and only if $Z_i(u_1) = Z_j(u_2)$. Since $\rVec{Z} = \rVec{Z}_V+\rVec{Z}_E$ with $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$ being mutually independent, a necessary condition is that $Z_{V,i}(u_1) = Z_{V,j}(u_2)$. Given the correlation structure (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) at the vertices, the variance-covariance matrix $\Tilde{\latMatr{K}}$ of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ is quasi-Laplacian (Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}) and thus it has only one null eigenvalue associated with the vector ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}$. That is, the only non-trivial linear combination of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ having a zero variance is, up to a constant factor, ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}^\top \rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$. Therefore, $Z_{V,i}(u_1) = Z_{V,j}(u_2)$ for $u_1, u_2 \in V$ only if $i=j$ and $u_1=u_2$. Given the linear interpolation on the edges (Equation (\ref{eq:interpZv})), the same holds true for any two points $u_1$ and $u_2$ belonging to $\mathcal G$. \item The claim stems from Equations (\ref{sympseudo}) and (\ref{eq:explicitWritingMultivMetric}). \item Let $u_0,u_1,\ldots,u_n \in \mathcal{G}$ and $\dVec{c}_1,\dots, \dVec{c}_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$. Let $\dVec{c}_0=-\latMatr{A}\sum_{i=1}^n \dVec{c}_i$, where $\latMatr{A}$ is a $p \times p$ matrix such that $\latMatr{A}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{p}} = {\mathbf{1}_{p}}$. Then, from Equation (\ref{eq:negativesemidef}), one has: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \sum_{i,j=0}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_j) \dVec{c}_j \\ &= \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_j) \dVec{c}_j + \sum_{i=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_0) \dVec{c}_0 + \sum_{j=1}^n \dVec{c}_0^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_0,u_j) \dVec{c}_j + \dVec{c}_0^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0) \dVec{c}_0\\ &= \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_j)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_0)\latMatr{A}-\latMatr{A}^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_j)+\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\latMatr{A}\right] \dVec{c}_j, \end{split} \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. }, the mapping $(u,v) \mapsto -[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u,v)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u,u_0)\latMatr{A}-\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,v)+\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\latMatr{A}]$ is positive semidefinite (Equation \ref{eq:positiveSemidef}). \item Taking $\dVec{c}_1 = \ldots = \dVec{c}_n := \dVec{c}$ and $\latMatr{A} {=\latMatr{I}_p}$, one gets \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \sum_{i,j=1}^n \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_j)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_j)+\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\right] \dVec{c}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Accounting for the fact that $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}^\top$ and $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_1)=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_2)$, one obtains, for $n=1$ and $u_0=u_2$: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)\right] \dVec{c}, \end{split} \end{equation*} and for $n=2$: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)+3\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)-2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_0)-2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_0)\right] \dVec{c}, \end{split} \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. }, $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)$ and $2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_0)+2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)-3\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)$ are positive semidefinite matrices. } \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Use properties of pseudo-variograms and the quasi-Laplacian vertex covariance; choose test vectors in the CNSD inequality.

Let us show that it is also necessary. From the definition of the pseudo-variogram as per Equation (\ref{eq:pseudoVariogramDef}), $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2) = 0$ if and only if $Z_i(u_1) = Z_j(u_2)$. Since $\rVec{Z} = \rVec{Z}_V+\rVec{Z}_E$ with $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$ being mutually independent, a necessary condition is that $Z_{V,i}(u_1) = Z_{V,j}(u_2)$. Given the correlation structure (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) at the vertices, the variance-covariance matrix $\Tilde{\latMatr{K}}$ of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ is quasi-Laplacian (Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}) and thus it has only one null eigenvalue associated with the vector ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}$. nodes.name: Claim: necessity
nodes.statement: Let us show that it is also necessary. From the definition of the pseudo-variogram as per Equation (\ref{eq:pseudoVariogramDef}), $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2) = 0$ if and only if $Z_i(u_1) = Z_j(u_2)$. Since $\rVec{Z} = \rVec{Z}_V+\rVec{Z}_E$ with $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$ being mutually independent, a necessary condition is that $Z_{V,i}(u_1) = Z_{V,j}(u_2)$. Given the correlation structure (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) at the vertices, the variance-covariance matrix $\Tilde{\latMatr{K}}$ of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ is quasi-Laplacian (Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}) and thus it has only one null eigenvalue associated with the vector ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}$. That is, the only non-trivial linear combination of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ having a zero variance is, up to a constant factor, ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}^\top \rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$. Therefore, $Z_{V,i}(u_1) = Z_{V,j}(u_2)$ for $u_1, u_2 \in V$ only if $i=j$ and $u_1=u_2$. nodes.name: Vertex covariance quasi-Laplacian: one null direction
nodes.statement: Given the correlation structure (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) at the vertices, the variance-covariance matrix $\Tilde{\latMatr{K}}$ of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ is quasi-Laplacian (Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}) and thus it has only one null eigenvalue associated with the vector ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}$. That is, the only non-trivial linear combination of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ having a zero variance is, up to a constant factor, ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}^\top \rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$. Therefore, $Z_{V,i}(u_1) = Z_{V,j}(u_2)$ for $u_1, u_2 \in V$ only if $i=j$ and $u_1=u_2$.

nodes.name: Choose c_0 = -A sum c_i in the CNSD inequality
nodes.statement: Let $u_0,u_1,\ldots,u_n \in \mathcal{G}$ and $\dVec{c}_1,\dots, \dVec{c}_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$. Let $\dVec{c}_0=-\latMatr{A}\sum_{i=1}^n \dVec{c}_i$, where $\latMatr{A}$ is a $p \times p$ matrix such that $\latMatr{A}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{p}} = {\mathbf{1}_{p}}$. Then, from Equation (\ref{eq:negativesemidef}), one has: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \sum_{i,j=0}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_j) \dVec{c}_j \\ &= \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_j) \dVec{c}_j + \sum_{i=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_0) \dVec{c}_0 + \sum_{j=1}^n \dVec{c}_0^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_0,u_j) \dVec{c}_j + \dVec{c}_0^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0) \dVec{c}_0\\ &= \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_j)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_0)\latMatr{A}-\latMatr{A}^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_j)+\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\latMatr{A}\right] \dVec{c}_j, \end{split} \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. }, the mapping $(u,v) \mapsto -[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u,v)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u,u_0)\latMatr{A}-\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,v)+\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\latMatr{A}]$ is positive semidefinite (Equation \ref{eq:positiveSemidef}).
nodes.statement_short: Choose c_0 = -A sum c_i in the CNSD inequality

nodes.name: Special choices n=1,2 give the two psd matrices
nodes.statement: Taking $\dVec{c}_1 = \ldots = \dVec{c}_n := \dVec{c}$ and $\latMatr{A} {=\latMatr{I}_p}$, one gets \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \sum_{i,j=1}^n \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_j)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_j)+\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\right] \dVec{c}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Accounting for the fact that $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}^\top$ and $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_1)=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_2)$, one obtains, for $n=1$ and $u_0=u_2$: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)\right] \dVec{c}, \end{split} \end{equation*} and for $n=2$: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)+3\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)-2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_0)-2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_0)\right] \dVec{c}, \end{split} \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. }, $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)$ and $2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_0)+2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)-3\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)$ are positive semidefinite matrices.

nodes.name: Vertex contribution equals delta' Sigma delta
nodes.statement: Thus, let us show that ${\latMatr{D}}_{ii}^V(u_1,u_2)=d_{R}^V(u_1,u_2)$. Let $u_1,u_2\in \mathcal G$ {and $k_{V,ii}$ be the $i$-th diagonal entry of {$\latMatr K_{\rVec{Z}_V}$}. Then, on account of Proposition \ref{prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE}}: \begin{align*} {\latMatr{D}}_{ii}^V(u_1,u_2)&=k_{V,ii}(u_1,u_1)+k_{V,ii}(u_2,u_2)-2k_{V,ii}(u_1,u_2)\\ &=\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}^\top \Tilde{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \dVec{\delta}_{1,V}+ \dVec{\delta}_{2,V}^\top \Tilde{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \dVec{\delta}_{2,V} -2 \dVec{\delta}_{1,V}^\top \Tilde{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \dVec{\delta}_{2,V}\\ &=\round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^\top \round{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}+k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}\\ &=\round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^\top {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}} + k_1\round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} \round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}\\ &=\round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^\top {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}, \end{align*} where in the last step we have used $\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \dVec{\delta}_{2,V}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = 1$ owing to Equation (\ref{eq:delta_i}).
nodes.statement_short: Vertex contribution equals delta' Sigma delta

nodes.name: Recall the Anderes et al. covariance Sigma_A
nodes.statement: It is left to show that this quantity coincides with the resistance counterpart of \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}. They define their covariance matrix, here denoted by ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}_{\latMatr{A}}$, as the (proper) inverse of a modified Laplacian matrix $\latMatr{L}$, where a one has been added on an arbitrary diagonal entry. In formulae: ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}_{\latMatr{A}}:=({\latMatr{L}}+\dVec e_j \dVec e_j^\top)^{-1}$, where $\dVec e_j$ is the $j^\text{th}$ vector of the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$. It follows directly from \citet[Equation 13]{anderes_isotropic_2020} that $d_{R}^V=\round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^\top {\grMatr{\Sigma}}_{\latMatr{A}} \round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}$.\par
nodes.statement_short: Recall the Anderes et al. covariance Sigma_A

nodes.name: Claim: rank-one updates do not change the quadratic form

Firstly, let us show that the hypotheses of the theorem are satisfied: we have to prove that $\dVec x
ot\in R({\latMatr{L}})$, where $R$ denotes the range or column space. $R({\latMatr{L}})$ is perpendicular to the kernel of $\latMatr L$, that is (recall that $\latMatr L$ is a quasi-Laplacian matrix) $\ker({\latMatr{L}})=\curly{h\,{\mathbf{1}_{n}}\,:\,h\in\mathbb{R}}$. Now, $\dVec x\in R({\latMatr{L}})\iff \dVec x \perp \ker({\latMatr{L}}) \iff {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x=0$, yet ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x 
e 0$ by hypothesis. Therefore $\dVec x
ot\in R({\latMatr{L}})$, 	extit{i.e. } we can apply the above-mentioned theorem. In the following computations, we have adopted the notation used by \citet[Section 2]{meyer_generalized_1973}, 	extit{i.e. }:  egin{align*} \dVec k&:={\latMatr{L}}^-\dVec x & \dVec h&:=\dVec x^	op {\latMatr{L}}^-\ \dVec u&:=ound{\latMatr{I}_n-\latMatr L{\latMatr{L}}^-}\dVec x= rac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n	imes n}} \dVec x & \dVec v&:= \dVec x^	op ound{\latMatr{I}_n-{\latMatr{L}}^- \latMatr L} =  rac{1}{n} \dVec x^	op {\mathbf{1}_{n	imes n}}\  eta &:= 1+\dVec x^	op \latMatr L^- \dVec x. \end{align*} In addition, we have $
orm{\dVec u}^2=
orm{\dVec v}^2= \dVec u^	op \dVec u =  rac{1}{n^2}{\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op ({\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x)({\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x) {\mathbf{1}_{n}} =  rac{1}{n}({\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x)^2
e 0$. Let us finally apply Equation (3.1) of \cite{meyer_generalized_1973}:  egin{align*} ound{{\latMatr{L}}+\dVec x \dVec x^	op}^-&={\latMatr{L}}^- - \dVec k \dVec u^- - \dVec v^- \dVec h + eta \dVec v^- \dVec u^-\ &={\latMatr{L}}^-- rac{\dVec k\dVec u^	op}{
orm{\dVec u}^2} -  rac{\dVec v^	op \dVec h}{
orm{\dVec v}^2} +  eta  rac{\dVec v^	op \dVec u^	op}{
orm{\dVec v}^2 
orm{\dVec u}^2}\ &={\latMatr{L}}^- -  rac{{\latMatr{L}}^- \dVec x {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op}{{\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x} -  rac{{\mathbf{1}_{n}} \dVec x^	op {\latMatr{L}}^-}{{\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x} + ound{1+ \dVec x^	op {\latMatr{L}}^- \dVec x}  rac{{\mathbf{1}_{n	imes n}}}{ound{{\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x}^2}. \end{align*} To show (ef{eq:thesisRank1Update}), it is now sufficient to prove that  egin{equation*} ound{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^	op ound{ound{1+ \dVec x^	op {\latMatr{L}}^- \dVec x}  rac{{\mathbf{1}_{n	imes n}}}{ound{{\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x}^2}-  rac{{\latMatr{L}}^- \dVec x {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op}{{\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x} -  rac{{\mathbf{1}_{n}} \dVec x^	op {\latMatr{L}}^-}{{\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec x}}ound{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}=0. \end{equation*} It is possible to see this by noticing that ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op ound{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}={\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec{\delta}_{1,V} - {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^	op \dVec{\delta}_{2,V}= 1-1=0$ and similarly $ound{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^	op {\mathbf{1}_{n}}=0$, therefore each term of the above equation equals 0.
